directions.description: Gödel showed self-reference breaks completeness, but what if self-referential proofs are not paradoxes but VALID mathematical objects? Develop a proof theory where proofs can reference their own structure — a proof of theorem T can contain a subproof that assumes T as a hypothesis, forming a circular dependency that is resolved through a fixed-point construction. Conjecture: Non-well-founded proofs form a convergent fixed point under a natural topolog: the space of proof trees with the tree topology is a Scott domain, and self-referential proofs correspond to infinite chains whose lub is a valid proof. A proof that references itself is like a recursive function: it converges if the self-reference occurs at a strictly smaller ordinal. Test: formalize non-well-founded proof trees as coinductive types in Lean 4, prove that the proof of 'P implies P' by assuming P is a valid non-well-founded proof with ordinal height 1, and show that the liar sentence 'this statement is unprovable' is NOT a valid non-well-founded proof because its ordinal height is undefined. Impact: turns the liar paradox from a bug into a feature — self-referential proofs are a new class of mathematical object with their own consistency conditions.
directions.proof_strategy: Define NWFP (non-well-founded proofs) as coinductive types: a proof is a tree where children are proofs, but cycles are allowed as long as each cycle has decreasing ordinal rank. Define ordinal height: oh(P) = sup{oh(Q)+1 : Q is a subproof of P}. A NWFP is valid if oh(P) is a well-defined ordinal. Prove consistency: if NWFP proves False, then oh(False) < oh(False), contradiction. Prove completeness: every true Pi_1 sentence has a NWFP of finite height. Test: formalize in Lean 4 and verify the P-implies-P example.
directions.title: Non-Well-Founded Proofs: Proofs That Reference Themselves

directions.description: The integers Z live on a line, but what happens to arithmetic on a curved space? Define hyperbolic integers Z_H as the set of points in the Poincaré disk that are images of Z under a discrete subgroup Gamma of PSL(2,R). Define hyperbolic primes as the vertices of the tessellation induced by Gamma, and hyperbolic addition/multiplication via the group action. Conjecture: Z_H has unique factorization into hyperbolic primes, and the hyperbolic prime number theorem holds: the number of hyperbolic primes in a hyperbolic disk of radius R is asymptotic to R^2 / (2 log R). The hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum_{n in Z_H, |n|_H > 0} 1/|n|_H^{2s} satisfies a functional equation and has zeros only on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. Test: compute zeta_H(s) for the modular group Gamma = PSL(2,Z) and verify that the first 100 zeros lie on Re(s) = 1/2. Impact: number theory on curved spaces — where primes are geometric objects and the Riemann Hypothesis might be PROVABLE.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z_H as the orbit of 0 under Gamma = PSL(2,Z) acting on the Poincaré disk. Define |n|_H as the hyperbolic distance from the origin. Prove Z_H is a discrete subset of the disk. Define the hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum 1/|n|_H^{2s} and prove it converges for Re(s) > 1. Prove the functional equation zeta_H(s) = pi^{s-1/2} Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(s/2) zeta_H(1-s) using Selberg's trace formula. Test: compute first 100 zeros numerically and verify Re(s) = 1/2.
directions.title: Hyperbolic Number Theory: Arithmetic on the Poincaré Disk

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers are the largest ordered field, containing every real number and infinitely many infinities and infinitesimals. But what if a surreal number could be in SUPERPOSITION — simultaneously equal to multiple values until observed? Define quantum surreal numbers as surreal-valued quantum states: |psi> = sum_i alpha_i |No_i> where No_i are surreal numbers and alpha_i are complex amplitudes. Conjecture: The quantum surreal field Q(No) is a non-Archimedean quantum field where the spectral theorem extends: every self-adjoint operator on a quantum surreal Hilbert space has a spectral decomposition into surreal-valued projections. The key insight is that infinitesimal surreal numbers provide a natural framework for quantum measurement: the probability of observing |No_i> is not alpha_i^2 (which may be infinitesimal) but the standard part of alpha_i^2. Test: construct the quantum surreal number |psi> = (1/sqrt(2))|0> + (1/sqrt(2))|epsilon> where epsilon is an infinitesimal surreal, and prove that measuring |psi> gives 0 with probability st(1/2) = 1/2 and epsilon with probability st(1/2 * epsilon^2) = 0 — the infinitesimal is unobservable! Impact: a mathematical framework where quantum mechanics and non-Archimedean analysis meet, giving infinitesimal probabilities a rigorous treatment.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Q(No) as the tensor product of the surreal field No with the complex numbers C. Define quantum surreal Hilbert space H_Q(No) as the completion of Q(No)^n with respect to the surreal-valued inner product. Prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on H_Q(No) by transfinite induction on the birthday of the surreal eigenvalues. The key lemma: if A is self-adjoint with surreal eigenvalues, then A = integral lambda dE(lambda) where E(lambda) are projections and lambda ranges over surreal numbers up to the birthday of A. Test: construct the 2x2 example and verify measurement probabilities.
directions.title: Quantum Surreal Numbers: Superposition of All Real Numbers

directions.description: Zero-knowledge proofs let you convince someone a statement is true without revealing WHY. Apply this to mathematics: a zero-knowledge proof of a theorem T convinces the verifier that T is provable in PA without revealing any step of the proof. Conjecture: Every theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic has a zero-knowledge proof whose communication complexity is polynomial in the length of the theorem statement (not the proof). This follows from the PCP theorem combined with the fact that PA-proofs can be arithmetized. The zero-knowledge protocol: (1) Prover commits to each proof step using a collision-resistant hash. (2) Verifier randomly challenges one proof step. (3) Prover opens that step and shows it follows from the axioms. Repeating O(k) times gives soundness error 2^{-k}. The proof is zero-knowledge because the verifier only sees one random step per challenge. Test: implement a zero-knowledge proof system for propositional tautologies and prove that a verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the tautology. Impact: mathematicians can certify results without revealing their methods — a mathematical equivalent of sealed-bid auctions for proof strategies.
directions.proof_strategy: Arithmetize PA-proofs: encode each proof step as a polynomial equation over a finite field F_p. Apply the PCP theorem: every NP statement has a probabilistically checkable proof of constant query complexity. Convert the PCP to zero-knowledge using the Fiat-Shamir heuristic: the prover commits to the PCP oracle, the verifier sends a random challenge, and the prover responds with a proof that is zero-knowledge by the hiding property of the commitment. Prove soundness: a cheating prover must fool the verifier with probability at most 2^{-k}. Prove zero-knowledge: the simulator can generate indistinguishable transcripts without the proof. Test: implement for propositional resolution proofs of length up to 1000.
directions.title: Zero-Knowledge Theorem Proving: I Can Prove Fermat's Last Theorem Without Showing You the Proof

directions.description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.
directions.proof_strategy: Define B = {0,...,24}^{1312000} as the Library. Compute |B| = 25^{1312000}. Define the meaning probability P(T) = sum_{b in B: b contains proof of T} 1/|B|. Prove P(T) >= |T| * 25^{-k(T)} where k(T) is the Kolmogorov complexity of T. Construct a distributed catalog using de Bruijn sequences: encode each volume's address as a substring of a de Bruijn sequence B(25, m) for m = ceil(log_{25}(1312000)). Prove the catalog requires N >= 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_{25}(2)) volumes. Test: implement the mini-Library with alphabet 4, book length 16, and compute meaning probabilities.
directions.title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library

directions.description: We conjecture that the finite Chromonic Lemma extends to infinite, locally finite, strongly connected digraphs. Formally, let G be an infinite directed graph that is strongly connected and locally finite, equipped with a real‑valued weight function on its edges and a color‑blending operation satisfying the Color Blend Axiom. If there exists a vertex coloring c : V → Colors such that for every vertex v, c(v) equals the weighted blend of the colors of its out‑neighbors (i.e., c(v) = π_{(u,p)∈Out(v)} p·c(u) ), then c must be constant. This generalizes the paper’s result from finite graphs to infinite ones and highlights the robustness of the underlying combinatorial principle.

   (∀ v, c v = blend (λ u => (w (G.edge v u), c u))) → (∀ v, c v = c (Classical.arbitrary V)) := by

   -- 2. By the finite Chromonic Lemma, each G_n forces c|_{V_n} constant.
   -- 3. Use an ultralimit of the constants to obtain a global constant.

The Color Blend Axiom ensures the limit respects blending, and strong connectivity yields a contradiction unless the coloring is constant. Alternatively, formulate the condition as a fixed‑point equation on the space of colorings and apply a Banach‑type contraction argument using the weights and the axiom.

Conjecture: For any fixed integer r≥2 and any collection of graphs H1, …, Hr, let ψ = ∥_{j=1}^r (ω67(Hj)‑1). Define the critical edge density π_c = 1‑1/ψ. For a host graph G0 on n vertices with edge density exactly π_c−ε (for a fixed ε>0) consider the random‑perturbation model where we add m random edges (without replacement). Then the minimal number of edges that forces the perturbed graph to be (H1, …, Hr)_v‑Ramsey satisfies

    m_c(n) = π_c * (n choose 2) + Ψ(n^{3/2}),

and there is a sharp threshold: if m = m_c(n) + ω(n^{3/2}) then with high probability the perturbed graph is (H1, …, Hr)_v‑Ramsey; if m = m_c(n) − ω(n^{3/2}) then with high probability it is not. Moreover, the window of size O(n^{3/2}) is the critical window for the transition.

directions.description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies). Moreover, every non-metrizable space requires at least 3 observers. The intuition: the real topology is what ALL observers agree on, and phantom topologies are what individual observers see. Like quantum mechanics, measurement changes the topology. Test: prove that R with the standard topology is the intersection of the lower limit topology and the upper limit topology (2 observers). Prove that the Zariski topology on R^2 requires at least 3 observers. Impact: a new notion of topology where the space itself depends on the observer — the mathematical formalization of 'reality depends on the observer'.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a phantom topology as a function T: O -> Top(X) from a set of observers to topologies on X. Define the intersection topology T_cap = intersection of all T(o). Prove: every second-countable T_0 space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with |O| = 2. Proof: for a basis {B_n}, define T(o1) as the topology generated by {B_n : n odd} union {X} and T(o2) by {B_n : n even} union {X}. Then T_cap = tau. Prove non-metrizable spaces need >= 3 observers: the Zariski topology on R^2 cannot be written as the intersection of two first-countable topologies. Test: verify the R example and construct the 3-observer phantom representation for the Zariski topology.
directions.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them

directions.description: A vampire number is a composite number v with an even number of digits that can be factizedd as v = x * y where x and y together have the same digits as v. The smallest is 1260 = 21 * 60. But vampire numbers are just the beginning. Define: (1) Werewolf numbers: v = x * y where x and y share exactly one digit with v. (2) Ghost numbers: v = x * y where v has NO digits in common with x or y. (3) Zombie numbers: v = x * y where x and y are both prime (these violate the definition but exist — 125460 = 204 * 615 = 246 * 510, where both factorizations involve a prime and a composite). Conjecture: The density of vampire numbers in [10^{2n}, 10^{2n+1}] approaches 1/sqrt(n) as n -> infinity. Every even-length interval [10^{2k}, 10^{2k+2}] contains at least one vampire number. Ghost numbers have density 0 — they become vanishingly rare as the number of digits increases. Test: enumerate all vampire, werewolf, ghost, and zombie numbers up to 10^8. Prove the density conjecture by counting valid digit permutations. Impact: a playful but genuine number theory of arithmetic creatures — combinatorial digit problems that are easy to state but may be as hard as factoring.
directions.proof_strategy: Define vampire numbers formally: v is a vampire number iff v has 2n digits and there exist x, y each with n digits such that v = x*y and the multiset of digits of v equals the union of digits of x and y. Count the number of digit arrangements: for a 2n-digit number with distinct digits, there are C(2n, n) * n! * n! possible fang pairs, so the expected number of fang pairs is C(2n, n) * (n!)^2 / 10^{2n} = C(2n,n) / 10^n ~ 1/sqrt(n). Prove existence in every interval by constructing explicit vampire numbers using the formula 1260 * 10^{2k} for k >= 0. Test: enumerate up to 10^8.
directions.title: Vampire Numbers and Other Numerical Monsters: A Bestiary of Arithmetic Oddities

directions.description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ... (each term avoids being the sum of the two previous terms). Conjecture: The anti-Fibonacci sequence A(n) grows as A(n) ~ n^2/4, and the ratio A(n)/n^2 converges to 1/4. More precisely, A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1). The sequence avoids the golden ratio entirely — the ratio A(n+1)/A(n) does NOT converge, instead oscillating between 1 and 2. The complement of the anti-Fibonacci sequence (numbers that ARE sums of two previous anti-Fibonacci numbers) has density 0. Test: compute A(n) for n up to 10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 approaches 1/4. Prove A(n) = floor(n^2/4) + O(1) by induction. Impact: a beautiful counterpoint to the Fibonacci sequence — instead of converging to a constant, it grows quadratically while systematically avoiding addition.
directions.proof_strategy: Define A(1) = A(2) = 1, A(n+1) = smallest positive integer not equal to A(n) + A(n-1). Prove by strong induction: A(n) >= floor(n^2/4). Base: A(1)=1 >= 0, A(2)=1 >= 1. Inductive step: if A(k) >= floor(k^2/4) for k <= n, then A(n) + A(n-1) >= floor(n^2/4) + floor((n-1)^2/4), so A(n+1) <= A(n) + A(n-1) - 1 + delta where delta accounts for gaps, giving A(n+1) >= floor((n+1)^2/4). Prove A(n) <= ceil(n^2/4) + 1 by showing the avoidance constraint only blocks one value per step. Test: compute A(n) for n=1..10^6 and verify A(n)/n^2 -> 1/4.
directions.title: The Anti-Fibonacci Sequence: Numbers That Avoid the Golden Ratio at All Costs

directions.description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
directions.proof_strategy: Define an Escher staircase in ring R as a strictly ascending chain I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... such that intersection of I_n is contained in I_1. Prove Int(Z) has an Escher staircase: I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z}. Each I_n is strictly contained in I_{n+1} (the polynomial x choose n is in I_{n+1} but not I_n). Intersection of I_n = {0} contained in I_1. Prove k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n: the chain (x_1) contained in (x_1,x_2) contained in ... contained in (x_1,...,x_n) has length n. Prove Z_p has no Escher staircase (Noetherian). Test: verify for Int(Z) and k[x,y,z].
directions.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back

directions.description: Deja vu — the feeling that you've experienced something before — is a fixed point in a dynamical system. Model cognitive state as a function f: S -> S mapping current brain state to next brain state. A deja vu is a state s such that f^n(s) = s for some n > 0 — a periodic point of the cognitive dynamical system. Conjecture: By Sharkovsky's theorem, the existence of a period-3 orbit in the cognitive dynamics (three distinct states that cycle) implies chaos in the sense of Li-Yorke, meaning there exist uncountably many cognitive trajectories that are neither periodic nor convergent. Moreover, the set of deja vu states (periodic points of f) is dense in the cognitive state space S if f is continuous and S is an interval. The frequency of deja vu (occurring in ~70% of people) corresponds to the natural density of periodic points in a typical chaotic map. Test: model cognitive dynamics as a logistic map f(x) = rx(1-x) on [0,1] with parameter r chosen to match empirical deja vu frequencies. For r = 3.83 (period-3 window), compute the density of periodic points and compare to the 70% lifetime incidence. Impact: deja vu is not a glitch — it's a mathematical inevitability of continuous cognitive dynamics. Any continuous cognitive map with a period-3 orbit MUST have deja vu.
directions.proof_strategy: Model cognitive state space as S = [0,1] and cognitive dynamics as f: S -> S continuous. Apply Sharkovsky's theorem: if f has a point of period 3, then f has points of all periods. A deja vu state is a periodic point: s such that f^n(s) = s. Prove: the set of periodic points is dense in S for the logistic map at r = 3.83. Compute the density of periodic points: PeriodicPoints_n(f) / n approaches the topological entropy h(f) as n -> infinity. For the logistic map at r = 3.83, h(f) ~ 0.38. The lifetime incidence of deja vu (~70%) is consistent with the probability that a random orbit encounters a periodic point neighborhood within a typical observation window. Test: simulate 10000 random orbits of the logistic map and count how many encounter periodic neighborhoods.
directions.title: The Mathematics of Deja Vu: Fixed Points in Consciousness and Cognition

directions.description: For every regular graph $G$ of degree $d\ge 2$ (i.e., $\Delta(G)=d$ and $G$ is $d$‑regular), we conjecture that the central graph $C(G)$ achieves the maximal possible AVD‑total chromatic number, namely $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) = d+3$, except in the degenerate case where $G$ is a complete graph $K_{d+1}$ (for which $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) = d+2$). This conjecture refines the already verified AVD‑TCC bound for central graphs of regular graphs and predicts exact values.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem avd_total_chromatic_number_central_regular
  {V : Type*} [fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) (d : ℕ)
  (h_reg : G.is_regular d)
  (h_not_complete : ¬ G.is_complete)
  : avd_total_chromatic_number (central_graph G) = d + 3 :=
begin
  -- Outline:
  -- 1. Show lower bound via a subgraph H of C(G) with χ''_a(H) = d+3.
  -- 2. Construct explicit AVD‑total coloring with d+3 colors.
  -- 3. Combine to obtain equality.
  sorry
end
directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture is approached in two parts. 1. **Lower bound**: Show that any AVD‑total coloring of $C(G)$ must use at least $d+3$ colors by constructing a small subgraph (e.g., a copy of $K_{d+1}$ or a suitable $d$‑regular subgraph) whose AVD‑total chromatic number is known to be $d+3$ (using results of Zhang et al. or the AVD‑TCC). This yields $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) \ge d+3$. 2. **Upper bound**: Build an explicit AVD‑total coloring of $C(G)$ with $d+3$ colors. The coloring proceeds by first coloring the original vertices of $G$ with $d+1$ colors respecting regularity, then extending to the subdivision vertices and the added universal edges in such a way that adjacent vertex colour‑sets remain distinct. The construction uses known colourings for regular graphs and the fact that $C(G)$ is obtained from $S(G)$ by joining non‑adjacent vertices, which simplifies the constraints. Combining both directions gives the desired equality (or the exceptional value for $K_{d+1}$).
directions.title: Exact AVD‑total chromatic number of central graphs of regular graphs

directions.description: We conjecture that for any oriented product structure \((A,B,P)\) of type \((m,n)\) with \(m,n\ge2\) satisfying the no‑fold condition \(\mathsf T_2\), the weighted dual Fisher inequality is strict unless \((m,n)=(2,2)\) and the structure is the affine plane of order 2 (i.e. the unique 2×2 grid). Moreover, if the middle‑link girth is 6 then the minimum of the two horizontal‑link girths is at most 4, and equality in the weighted dual Fisher inequality forces the structure to be exactly this affine‑plane construction. This would classify all extremal cases of the combinatorial inequalities underlying the taiko assembly theorem.

theorem weighted_dual_fisher_strict
  {m n : ℕ} (hmn : 2 ≤ m) (hn : 2 ≤ n)
  (hT2 : no_fold_condition (A B P))
  (hEquality : weighted_dual_fisher A B P = bound) :
    (m = 2 ∧ n = 2) ∧ is_affine_plane A B P
directions.proof_strategy: We would formalize the definition of an oriented product structure, its girth functions, the no‑fold condition, and the weighted dual Fisher inequality in Lean. Then we would perform a computer‑assisted search over all product structures with support sizes up to a reasonable bound (e.g. \(m,n\le 10\)). For each candidate we check the inequality; any case attaining equality is recorded. Using combinatorial reasoning (product identity, pressure inequalities, Fisher bounds) we would then prove that any equality case must have \(m=n=2\) and be isomorphic to the 2×2 affine plane. The search provides falsifying examples if the conjecture is false, while the reasoning supplies a proof of the classification.
directions.title: Equality case of the weighted dual Fisher inequality for taiko product structures

directions.description: For any finite antipodal set X on the d-dimensional sphere (d ≥ 2), if the harmonic strength Hst(X) contains any even integer, then it must contain 2. This would imply that the smallest even degree in the harmonic strength of an antipodal design is always 2.

directions.proof_strategy: Investigate the relationship between the moment tensors of antipodal sets. For an antipodal set X, the sum of harmonic polynomials of degree 2k is related to the 2k-th moment tensor. If all odd moments vanish (by antipodality), the condition for degree 2 to be in Hst(X) is that the inertia tensor is proportional to the identity. If degree 2 is not in Hst(X), the inertia tensor has distinct eigenvalues. Use representation theory of O(d+1) to show that if a higher even moment vanishes, then the inertia tensor must be isotropic, forcing degree 2 to vanish. Alternatively, construct a counterexample by finding an antipodal set with Hst(X) containing 4 but not 2.
directions.title: Even Harmonic Strength of Antipodal Spherical Designs Contains 2

directions.description: Conjecture: Let $f_{m_1, \mu_1}$ and $f_{m_2, \mu_2}$ be depth one mock modular Eisenstein series defined as in equation (1) with weights $\k_1$ and $\k_2$. Their coupling via the product $h(\t) := f_{m_1, \mu_1}(\t) \cdot f_{m_2, \mu_2}(\t)$ satisfies the depth two mock modularity condition: the completion $\wh{h}(\t, \bar{\t})$ has a conjugate derivative $\frac{\del}{\del \bar{\t}} \wh{h} \in v^{-\k_1 - \k_2} \mathfrak{M}_{2\k_1 + 2\k_2 + 2} \otimes \overline{\mathfrak{M}_0} \oplus v^{-\k_1} \mathfrak{M}_{\k_1 + \k_2 + 1} \otimes \overline{\mathfrak{M}_1}$, where $\mathfrak{M}_r$ denotes modular forms of weight $r$.

  let f1 := depth_one_eisenstein m1 μ1 k1
  let f2 := depth_one_eisenstein m2 μ2 k2
  let h_completion := complexify (f1 * f2)
  in ∂ h_completion ∂ conj τ ∈
     v^(-k1 - k2) • M_(2*k1 + 2*k2 + 2) ⊗ M̄_0 ⊕
     v^(-k1) • M_(k1 + k2 + 1) ⊗ M̄_1

Use the known transformation laws for depth one forms and their non-holomorphic integrals to derive the depth two structure. 4. Apply the differential operators from Zwegers' lifting to confirm the shadow formula.

2) G is a near‑bipartite brick belonging to the class characterised in the main theorem of the paper (i.e. the complete description of near‑bipartite bricks for which every b‑invariant edge is forcing).

Equivalently, the deranged condition depends only on the number of blocks m and not on the block sizes, so that the distribution of block sizes in deranged unit-interval parking functions is proportional to the distribution in all unit-interval parking functions.

Alternatively, use the symbolic method with the exponential generating function e^{1-eˣ}/(2-eˣ) and track block sizes via the labeled construction of set partitions.

directions.description: We conjecture that for any prime p >= 3, integer base b >= 2 with p not dividing b, let l be the order of b modulo p and d = (p-1)/l. For each prime q dividing d let m_q be the exponent of q in d. Then there exist Dirichlet characters χ_{q,r} modulo p of order q^{m_q} (for 1 <= r <= m_q) such that the sum S of the repetend digits and the sum T of the squares of the digits satisfy S = (b-1)/2 * l + (b-1)/2 * Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=1}^{m_q} [B_{χ_{q,r}}]_0, T = (T_0 + T_1)/d + Σ_{q|d} Σ_{r=2}^{m_q} [T_{q,r}]_0 / q^{m_q - r + 1} + [T_d]_0 / 2, where the definitions of T_0,T_1,T_{q,r} are the same as in Theorem 2 with the appropriate characters. Consequently the variance V_l = T/l - (S/l)^2 admits a closed formula involving only generalized Bernoulli numbers of characters whose order divides d. This recovers the known formulas for l = p-1 and l = (p-1)/2, and extends the theory to arbitrary repetend lengths dividing p-1.

Using the orthogonality relations we reduce S and T to sums of generalized Bernoulli numbers B_chi for characters chi whose order divides d. directions.description: We conjecture that apart from integer scalar multiples of products of cyclotomic polynomials (which give rational multiples of τ for all root arguments), the only integer palindrome of degree 4 whose four zeros all lie on the unit circle but are not all cyclotomic is, up to an integer factor, the polynomial 62826 = 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3). Consequently any such unit palindrome of degree 4 must be associate either to a cyclotomic product or to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3).

theorem unit_palindrome_degree4_classifies :
  ∀ (a b c : ℤ),
    let P := a*X^4 + b*X^3 + c*X^2 + b*X + a in
    (∀ z, eval P z = 0 → |z| = 1) →
      (∃ (k : ℤ) (hk : k ≠ 0), (P = k • (2 * (X^2 + X + 1) * (3*X^2 - 2*X + 3)) ∨
        (∃ (k : ℤ) (hk : k ≠ 0), (P = k • (X^2 + X + 1) * (X^2 + 1) ∨
          (P = k • (X^2 + 1) * (X^2 + X + 1) ∨ …))))
directions.proof_strategy: For a degree‑4 palindrome P(x)=a x⁴+b x³+c x²+b x+a with integer coefficients, we replace x+1/x by u and obtain the Chebyshev transform Q(u)=a(u²−2)+b u+c. The condition that all roots of P lie on |x|=1 is equivalent to Q having all real roots in [−2,2]. By analysing the integer parameters (a,b,c) we obtain finitely many possibilities for Q. A case‑by‑case discriminant analysis shows that the only admissible Q‑roots are u∈{−2,−1,0,1,2} (giving cyclotomic cases) and u=2/3. The latter yields P associate to 2·Φ₃(x)·(3x²−2x+3). Niven’s theorem rules out any other rational u in (−2,2) that could give a rational multiple of τ, so no further unit palindromes exist. The whole argument can be formalised in Lean by enumerating the finitely many integer triples (a,b,c) with bounded size and checking the root conditions using algebraic number theory libraries.
directions.title: Unique exceptional integer palindromes of degree 4 with unit roots

The conjecture asserts that the minimal rank of an abelian group needed for an isometric embedding of G equals k = t - rank_{GF(2)}(A). Moreover, this bound is tight: no embedding into a Cayley graph of an abelian group of rank < k exists unless G has a very restricted structure (e.g., is a partial cube). The conjecture is falsifiable by constructing counterexamples where a lower‑dimensional embedding is possible, or by verifying the bound for all small graphs algorithmically.

directions.description: We conjecture that for any fixed escalation granularity m≥1, the misère P‑positions of the single‑theater escalation game (Definition 1) eventually follow a simple congruence modulo (m+1). Precisely, there exists an integer T(m) such that for every ladder length N≥T(m) and every remaining rung count r with 0≤ r≤ N, the position r is a P‑position under misère play if and only if r ≡ 0 (mod m+1). This strengthens Theorem 4.1 by asserting that the congruence holds for all sufficiently long ladders, not merely for the specific parameters considered in the paper.
domain_bridges: formal methods in combinatorial game theory
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem misere_ladder_congruence_eventual (m : ℕ) (hm : m ≥ 1) : 
  ∃ (T : ℕ), ∀ (N : ℕ), N ≥ T → ∀ (r : ℕ), r ≤ N → 
    (is_P_position r) ↔ (r % (m + 1) = 0)
where
  is_P_position : ℕ → Prop := λ r =>
    match r with
    | 0 => false          -- r = 0 is an N‑position under misère
    | _ =>
      let opts := { d : ℕ | d ∈ escalation_set m ∧ d ≤ r } in
      ∀ d in opts, is_N_position (r - d)
and
  is_N_position : ℕ → Prop := λ r => r = 0 ∨ ∃ d in escalation_set m, d ≤ r ∧ is_P_position (r - d)
with
  escalation_set (m : ℕ) : Set ℕ := {1, 2, …, m}
directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture can be approached by (1) implementing the misère subtraction game in Lean for arbitrary m and N, (2) brute‑forcing the P‑position classification for all m up to a reasonable bound (e.g., m≥1 0) and all N up to a few hundred, (3) detecting the eventual periodicity and the conjectured modulus (m+1) via algorithmic pattern detection, and (4) then attempting an inductive proof that the periodicity holds once N exceeds the observed threshold T(m). Counter‑examples would falsify the conjecture, while a successful inductive argument would establish it for all m.
directions.title: Eventual congruence of misère P‑positions in nuclear escalation ladders

directions.description: The paper establishes a central limit theorem for Steinhaus random multiplicative functions in short intervals [x, x+y] for all y → ∞ with y = o(x), with a precise normalization that differs from √y when y is close to x. A natural conjecture is that the same result holds for Rademacher random multiplicative functions, at least for y in the range where the interval [x, x+y] contains a positive proportion of squarefree numbers (which is known to hold for y ≫ x^{1/2} unconditionally, and for all y → ∞ under RH). Specifically, for a Rademacher random multiplicative function f, and any y = y(x) with y → ∞, y = o(x), and such that the number of squarefree integers in [x, x+y] is (6/π²)y + o(y) with probability 1 - o(1), the normalized sum (1/σ(x,y)) ∑_{x≤n≤x+y} f(n) converges in distribution to N(0,1), where σ(x,y)² = Var(∑_{x≤n≤x+y} f(n)) has the same asymptotic as in the Steinhaus case.
domain_bridges: Limit theorems for dependent random variables

Show that the covariance structure of the Rademacher function restricted to squarefree integers matches that of the Steinhaus function, and that the contribution from intervals with few squarefree numbers is negligible in the limit. Use the fact that the characteristic function of the Rademacher sum can be approximated by that of the Steinhaus sum conditioned on squarefree support.

directions.description: For every integer k ≥ 6 with k ≡ 2 (mod 4), and for every pair of nonnegative integers (a, b) with a + b = k and a ≥ 1, the number 2^a · 3^b − 1 is composite. This formalizes the paper's theorem that row k of the principal skeleton L₁ contains no primes when k ≡ 2 (mod 4) and k ≥ 6. The proof exploits that k even forces a and b to share parity. When both even, 2^a · 3^b − 1 = (2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} − 1)(2^{a/2} · 3^{b/2} + 1) via difference of squares, with both factors > 1 for k ≥ 6. When both odd, k ≡ 2 (mod 4) forces a ≡ b (mod 4), yielding 2^a · 3^b ≡ 1 (mod 5) so 5 | (2^a · 3^b − 1), and the cofactor exceeds 1 since k ≥ 6 excludes the case a = b = 1 where the value equals 5.

directions.description: The minimal absolute value σ₅(n) of a non-vanishing sum of n fifth roots of unity is monotone non-increasing over congruence classes of n modulo 5. Furthermore, a strict decrease σ₅(n) > σ₅(n+5) occurs if and only if n+5 is of the form 5Fₘ, Lₘ, or 2Lₘ for some positive integer m, where Fₘ and Lₘ denote the m-th Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, respectively.

open Complex

def isFifthRootSum (n : ℕ) (s : ℂ) : Prop :=
  ∃ a : Fin 5 → ℕ, (∑ i, (a i : ℂ)) = n ∧ 
    s = a 0 + (a 1) * exp (2 * π * I / 5) + (a 2) * exp (4 * π * I / 5) + 
        (a 3) * exp (6 * π * I / 5) + (a 4) * exp (8 * π * I / 5)

  sInf { r : ℝ | ∃ s, isFifthRootSum n s ∧ s ≠ 0 ∧ r = ‖s‖ }

/-- Lucas numbers -/

  | 0 => 2
  | 1 => 1

This improves the Peres–Schlag exponent 2l to l+1, matching the sharp finite-field threshold established in the paper. The case l=1 is excluded since 2l = l+1 = 2 is already sharp by Besicovitch–Mattila constructions. For l ≥ 2, the gap between the known bound 2l and the conjectured bound l+1 remains open, and the paper's finite-field result strongly suggests l+1 is the true threshold.

    ∀ᵐ V ∂(grassmannMeasure n l),
      (interior (orthogonalProjection V '' E)).Nonempty := by

To lift this to ℝⁿ: (1) discretize the Euclidean problem by replacing E with a δ-packing and passing to a finite-field model via rescaling and reduction mod p, (2) apply the finite-field sharp threshold result to obtain rich projections for the discretized set, (3) use Bourgain's framework reformulating Peres–Schlag in terms of L² bounds for maximal k-plane transforms controlled by Riesz energy, (4) combine with the best available Kakeya maximal L^p estimates (from BCCLXZ and related works) and the paper's maximal k-plane transform bounds to close the gap from 2l down to l+1. Guth's polynomial partitioning method may provide the continuous analogue of the polynomial method used in the finite-field setting.

directions.description: We conjecture that for each integer n≥3 the exponent 3/(2n‑1) in the finite‑field Peres‑Schlag theorem for product sets is optimal. More precisely, there exists a constant c_n > 0 such that for all sufficiently large primes p there is a subset A ⊂ ℤ_p with |A| ≤ c_n·p^{3/(2n‑1)} for which no choice of coefficients t_1,…,t_n ∈ ℤ_p yields a covering t_1A + … + t_nA = ℤ_p. Equivalently, the threshold cannot be lowered below 3/(2n‑1).

    exists (c : Q), (0 < c) /
      forall (A : Finset (Zmod p)),
        (A.card <= c * (p : Q) ^ (3/(2*n - 1 : Q))) ->
          not (exists (t : Fin n -> Zmod p), forall (x : Zmod p), x ∈ (t 0).smul A + … + (t (n-1)).smul A)

A successful construction would establish the sharpness of the exponent 3/(2n‑1). A disproof would require showing that any set of size ≈ p^{3/(2n‑1)} inevitably yields a covering, perhaps via Fourier‑analytic or algebraic‑geometric methods.

Specifically, k_t(G) / n^t ≥ F_t(F_s^{-1}(k_s(G) / n^s)). This encompasses Reiher's clique density theorem as a special case when s=2.

Define the piecewise linear function L_{s,r} and prove Bollobás's original piecewise-linear interpolation bound. Define the Lovász-Simonovits clique density function F_r and its generalized inverse F_s^{-1}. Let $M(t)$ be the $g \times g$ Cartier-Manin matrix of the hyperelliptic curve $y^2 = x^d + \alpha x + t$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$. The determinant $\det(M(t))$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_p[t]$.

directions.description: For a geometric family of principally polarized abelian varieties over Q, the average size of the ℓ-Selmer group is unbounded if and only if the product of local Tamagawa ratios exceeds 1. Specifically, for the family of quadratic twists {E_d : d squarefree} of an elliptic curve E/Q at a prime ℓ of good reduction, the average |Sel_ℓ(E_d)| over |d| ≤ X is unbounded as X → ∞ if and only if ∏_p c_p(E, ℓ) > 1, where c_p(E, ℓ) is the local factor from the Greenberg–Wiles formula. The paper proves this for families with constant ℓ-torsion Galois module; the conjecture asserts it holds unconditionally.

Use the Greenberg-Wiles formula to express |Sel_ℓ(A)|/|Sel_ℓ(A^∨)^∨| = ∏_p c_p. For principally polarized varieties, the Cassels pairing gives |Sel_ℓ(A)| ≥ √(∏_p c_p). The key step is showing that the dual Selmer correction factor is bounded on average across the family, using the character sum and ramification section machinery developed in the paper to control the discrepancy between the local lower bound and the true Selmer size.
directions.title: Tamagawa Ratio Criterion for Unbounded Selmer Moments

This removes the 'no exceptional primes' condition from the paper's Corollary 1.3 and the 'sufficiently large prime factors' condition from Theorem 1.1, yielding the full generalization of the David-Fearnley-Kisilevsky conjecture from quadratic to all finite abelian extensions.

directions.description: The paper proves that a countable FAC poset P satisfies the Aharoni-Korman conjecture if P contains no saturated chain D such that either D or its reverse D* is of the form ⊕_{x∈ω} D_x, where each D_x is infinite and co-wellfounded. The conjecture asserts that this condition is also necessary: if a countable FAC poset P does contain such a saturated chain, then P fails to satisfy the Aharoni-Korman conjecture. This would yield a complete characterization of which countable FAC posets satisfy the Aharoni-Korman conjecture.

directions.description: For any convex polytope P in ℝ^� (with e = d+1 being the embedding dimension), the set of centerpoints of P coincides with the floating body of P at level 1/(d+1). Specifically, a point x is a centerpoint of P (meaning every closed halfspace containing x contains at least a 1/(d+1) fraction of the volume of P) if and only if x belongs to the floating body F_{1/(d+1)}(P), defined as the intersection of all closed halfspaces H⁺ such that vol(P \ H⁺) ≤ (1/(d+1)) · vol(P). The paper establishes this equivalence and further shows that for polytopes this set is semialgebraic.
domain_bridges: Convex geometry ↔ Combinatorial topology ↔ Semialgebraic geometry ↔ Measure theory on polytopes

directions.proof_strategy: The proof proceeds by double inclusion. (⊆): If x is a centerpoint, then every halfspace H⁺ containing x satisfies vol(P ∩ H⁺) ≥ vol(P)/(d+1), equivalently vol(P \ H⁺) ≤ vol(P)·d/(d+1); but the floating body condition requires vol(P \ H⁺) ≤ vol(P)/(d+1) for the halfspaces defining it, so one must show that a centerpoint lies in every halfspace whose complementary cap has volume ≤ vol(P)/(d+1). (⊇): Conversely, if x ∈ F_{1/(d+1)}(P), then x lies in every halfspace H⁺ with vol(P \ H⁺) ≤ vol(P)/(d+1), and one must show this forces every halfspace through x to capture at least 1/(d+1) of the volume. The key technical ingredient is that the cap-volume function is piecewise rational on the arrangement of oriented hyperplanes determined by the polytope's facets, which makes both sets explicitly semialgebraic and allows their coincidence to be verified.

directions.description: For a squarefree integer N > 1 with an even number of prime factors, and a positive divisor d | N, let w_d denote the corresponding Atkin-Lehner involution on the Shimura curve X_N. The genus of the quotient X_N / ⟨w_d⟩ is determined by the Riemann-Hurwitz formula applied to the double cover X_N → X_N / ⟨w_d⟩, where the number of fixed points of w_d equals the number of optimal embeddings of a certain quadratic order into the quaternion order, expressible via class numbers. The conjecture is: X_N / ⟨w_d⟩ has genus zero if and only if (N, d) belongs to an explicit finite list, which strictly contains the list {(6,6), (10,10), (22,22)} arising from genus-zero X_N alone. This classification is the key structural result enabling the extension of the Giampietro-Darmon factorization beyond the original conjecture.

Then formalize the fixed-point count of Atkin-Lehner involutions w_d in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders via optimal embedding counts. Apply Riemann-Hurwitz to the double cover X_N → X_N/⟨w_d⟩ to obtain the genus of the quotient. Finally, enumerate all pairs (N, d) with N squarefree, ω(N) even, d | N, for which the resulting genus is zero, yielding the explicit finite classification.

directions.description: The paper establishes that the diameter of the connected component of the chord swap graph on chord diagrams of size n and genus g (for n > 2g) is bounded above by C(n + g^2) for some universal constant C > 0. We conjecture that this universal constant can be taken to be exactly 1, yielding a tight diameter upper bound of precisely n + g^2.

This would establish the diameter bound via the triangle inequality. directions.description: For any split connected reductive group G over Q_p with Borel subgroup B and maximal torus T, the trianguline variety Y^{tri}(G) is Cohen-Macaulay. This strengthens the normality results established by Breuil-Hellmann-Schraen (for GL_n) and generalized in this paper (to arbitrary split reductive G, at certain points outside the smooth locus). Since Y^{tri}(G) is smooth of dimension dim(B) = dim(T) + |Φ^+| over the regular locus, Cohen-Macaulayness would follow from Serre's criterion (S2) combined with (R1) regularity in codimension 1. The (S2) condition is the deeper claim: for every point x ∈ Y^{tri}(G) with local ring O_{Y^{tri},x}, and every regular sequence f_1,...,f_d in the maximal ideal, the quotient O_{Y^{tri},x}/(f_1,...,f_d) has depth exactly d. This would imply the existence of well-behaved dualizing complexes and resolve the singularities of Y^{tri}(G) in the sense of local Langlands.

  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Step 1: Formalize the trianguline variety Y^{tri}(G) as a rigid analytic space parameterizing trianguline G-representations with their triangulation data, using the Tannakian formalism for Rep_L(G) developed in the paper. Step 2: Establish that Y^{tri}(G) is regular in codimension ≤ 1 (condition R1) by analyzing the singular locus—its complement is the smooth regular locus characterized by the regularity of the triangulation parameter δ: T(Z_p) → T(E), and the singular locus has codimension ≥ 2 by dimension counting via the root structure of G. Step 3: Prove condition (S2) by showing that for every point x with codim ≥ 2, the local ring O_{Y^{tri},x} satisfies depth ≥ min(2, dim O_{Y^{tri},x}), using the crystallinity criterion for (φ,Γ)-modules with G-structure established in the paper to control the local equations. Step 4: Apply Serre's criterion (R1 + S2 ⟹ normal + CM for equidimensional schemes) to conclude.
directions.title: Cohen-Macaulay Property of the Trianguline Variety for Reductive Groups

Show that a subspace failing to cyclically cover F_q^n implies the existence of a vector outside the union of its cyclic shifts, which translates under orthogonal complementation to a nonzero cyclic code lacking any full-weight codeword, and vice versa.

directions.description: The maximum of the logarithm of the absolute value of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line over the interval [T, 2T], defined as M_T = max_{t ∈ [T, 2T]} log|ζ(1/2 + it)|, satisfies the convergence in distribution: M_T - log(log(T)) + (3/2)log(log(log(T))) converges to the sum of two independent Gumbel random variables as T → ∞. This captures the extreme value statistics of the number-theoretic analogue to the black hole microstate counts proposed in the paper.

directions.description: The paper proves that the Aharoni-Korman conjecture holds for countable FAC posets containing no saturated chain D such that D or its reverse is of the form ⨁ D_x (where each D_x is infinite and co-wellfounded). Since any well-founded poset cannot contain such a chain D (as it would entail an infinite descending chain), the theorem implies the conjecture holds for all countable well-founded FAC posets. This conjecture proposes that the result extends to uncountable cardinals: every well-founded poset with no infinite antichains possesses a chain that meets every antichain in some partition of the poset into antichains.

directions.title: The Aharoni-Korman Conjecture for Well-Founded FAC Posets

The paper proves the Aharoni-Korman conjecture for countable FAC posets avoiding a specific chain obstruction (saturated chains of the form ⊕_{x∈ω} D_x with each D_x infinite and co-wellfounded). This conjecture extends the result to all well-founded FAC posets, regardless of cardinality, since well-foundedness eliminates infinite descending obstructing chains and structurally constrains ascending ones.

The key insight is that well-foundedness provides a rank function that naturally organizes the construction and prevents the specific chain obstruction identified in the paper.
directions.title: Aharoni-Korman Property for Well-Founded FAC Posets

The conjecture is that for m <= 4, gamma-positivity always holds: for every vector a in Z_{>=1}^4, the h*-polynomial of Q_{G(a)} is gamma-positive. This would yield a complete classification of gamma-positivity for this family.

For m = 4, compute the gamma-polynomial coefficients using the regular unimodular triangulation structure of symmetric edge polytopes and show all coefficients are non-negative. The linear and quadratic gamma-coefficients are already known positive; the key is controlling the cubic and higher terms via the combinatorics of the series-parallel structure.
directions.title: Gamma-positivity of symmetric edge polytopes for series-parallel graphs with at most four paths

directions.description: For even n ≥ 12, the unique extremal graph with T(n) edges and an edge of non-positive curvature has exactly two vertices of degree n-2 (forming the non-positive curvature edge) and all other vertices have degree n-1. This graph is obtained by removing n/2-2 disjoint edges from K_n such that no two removed edges share a vertex, and the two vertices of degree n-2 are adjacent.

Show that any graph with T(n) edges achieving the threshold must have exactly the specified degree distribution. Prove uniqueness by demonstrating that any two such extremal graphs are isomorphic via vertex relabeling. Use the relationship between graph curvature and Laplacian eigenvalues to constrain the possible structures.

directions.description: The trianguline variety X^{tri}_G associated to a split connected reductive group G over a p-adic field K is Cohen-Macaulay. Specifically, for every point x in X^{tri}_G with local ring O_{X^{tri}_G,x}, the depth equals the Krull dimension: depth(O_{X^{tri}_G,x}) = dim(O_{X^{tri}_G,x}). This extends the paper's results establishing smoothness on the very regular locus and normality at certain points outside this locus, predicting that all singularities are as mild as possible. Cohen-Macaulayness would imply full normality of X^{tri}_G (since CM implies Serre's condition S2, and the smooth locus has complement of codimension ≥ 2 by the regularity conditions on the triangulation parameter), strengthening the paper's partial normality result. It would also have significant consequences for the deformation theory of p-adic Galois representations with G-structure and for understanding the local Langlands correspondence via the geometry of the trianguline variety.

    [hK : IsAlgClosed (ResidueField K)]
    (X : TriangulineVariety G K) :
    CohenMacaulay X := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: The proof would proceed by analyzing the local structure of the trianguline variety at each point. Key steps: (1) On the very regular locus, the variety is smooth (proven in the paper), hence Cohen-Macaulay. (2) At singular points, use the Tannakian formalism developed in the paper to reduce to understanding the tangent cone in terms of root data. (3) The tangent cone at a singular point with parameter δ should be controlled by the roots α for which δ∘α∨ fails to be regular—these correspond to the walls of the Weyl chambers where smoothness breaks down. (4) Show that the defining ideal at each point is generated by a regular sequence of length equal to the codimension, leveraging the crystallinity criterion from the paper to explicitly describe the deformation ring. (5) The root system combinatorics (specifically, the Chevalley commutation relations and the structure of the unipotent radical) should ensure the regular sequence property holds via an inductive argument on the height of r
directions.title: Cohen-Macaulayness of the Trianguline Variety for Reductive Groups

directions.description: For every simple graph G with maximum degree Δ(G) > |V(G)|/3, the chromatic index χ'(G) equals Δ(G) if and only if G contains no Δ(G)-overfull subgraph (a subgraph H with |E(H)| > Δ(G)·⌊|V(H)|/2⌋). This would yield a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the chromatic index of dense graphs and implies several longstanding conjectures including the 1-Factorization Conjecture for regular graphs.

Prove key lemmas: (1) any Δ-overfull subgraph forces class 2, (2) the Petersen-minus-vertex P* is class 2 with no 3-overfull subgraph (showing Δ > |V|/3 is tight), (3) reduction to Δ-critical graphs. Then apply structural decomposition of critical graphs with Δ > |V|/3 to show they must contain overfull subgraphs, extending known results from Δ ≥ |V|−2 inward.
directions.title: The Overfull Conjecture

directions.description: For a prime p ≠ 2, a finite extension K of Q_p, and a set T = {a₀, b₀, ..., aᵍ, bᵍ} ⊂ P¹(K) of size 2g+2 with g ≥ 1, the set T is in good position (meaning Γ(T) = ⟨s₀,...,sᵍ⟩ is discontinuous and equals the free product ⟨s₀⟩*...*⟨sᵍ⟩, where each sᵢ has order 2 with fixed points {aᵢ,bᵢ}) if and only if: (1) the tree T(T) constructed from the reduction data is a path graph of length 2g+1, and (2) the p-adic valuations of the off-diagonal entries of normalized representatives of the sᵢ satisfy explicit contraction bounds ensuring the generators act as sufficiently contracting maps on the respective complementary residue disks in the Bruhat-Tits tree of PGL₂(K).

The backward direction (sufficiency) requires showing that when T(T) is a path of length 2g+1 and the contraction bounds hold, the group Γ(T) is free on the generators sᵢ: one analyzes the action on the Bruhat-Tits tree of PGL₂(K), showing that the contraction conditions force each reduced word in the sᵢ to act without fixed points in Ω_Γ, precluding any relations beyond sᵢ² = 1. The p-adic analytic estimates on matrix entries control how far the generators move points in the Bruhat-Tits tree, ensuring that compositions cannot create accidental fixed points.
directions.title: Tree-Contraction Characterization of Good Position for p-adic Schottky Groups

directions.description: The maximum fluctuation of log-microstate counts log Ω_N(E) over energy intervals of width O(√E) in large-N AdS/CFT belongs to the Fyodorov-Hiary-Keating universality class of Gaussian log-correlated fields. Specifically, defining M_N = max_{E ∈ [E₀, E₀ + δ]} log Ω_N(E) with δ ∝ √E₀ and E₀ ∝ N² (the black hole mass scale), the rescaled maximum (M_N - μ_N)/σ_N converges in distribution to a random variable with the modified Gumbel cumulative distribution function exp(-K·exp(-s)), where μ_N = (1/2)·S_N·log(S_N), σ_N = log(S_N), S_N ∝ N² is the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, and K > 0 is a universal constant determined by the log-correlated field covariance structure. This modified Gumbel with logarithmic correction factors distinguishes the FHK universality class from the classical Gumbel extreme value distribution and parallels the original FHK conjecture for max_t log|ζ(1/2+it)| on [0,T].

directions.proof_strategy: Establish the Gaussian log-correlated field structure of log Ω_N(E) via the holographic dictionary, identifying the covariance Cov(log Ω_N(E), log Ω_N(E')) ∼ log(N/|E-E'|) for nearby energies. Then apply the branching random walk / Gaussian multiplicative chaos framework to characterize the maximum: (1) prove the sub-leading order maximum concentrates via second moment method on the 'peaks' landscape of the log-correlated field; (2) establish the modified Gumbel tail by showing the maximum over dyadic mesoscopic intervals factorizes asymptotically (the decorrelation property); (3) identify the constant K via the local limit theorem for the number of high peaks. The key technical bridge is the equivalence between erratic N-dependence in AdS/CFT and the decorrelation of independent copies of the Gaussian model.
directions.title: FHK Universality Class for Black Hole Microstate Extreme Values

This is equivalent to the toric ideal of the matroid basis exchange ring being generated by quadratic binomials.

directions.title: White's Quadratic Exchange Conjecture (Part 3)

directions.description: For a finite poset P, the probabilistic powerdomain V1(P) is an RB-domain if and only if the local stochastic cone at every point of V1(P) is simplicial. This conjecture provides a geometric characterization of the RB-property that is equivalent to the combinatorial condition (P has a least element and its undirected Hasse graph is a tree) proven in the paper. It is falsifiable because one could exhibit a finite poset whose probabilistic powerdomain is an RB-domain but has a non-simplicial stochastic cone at some point, or vice versa.

directions.proof_strategy: The paper's Euclidean finite-step cone argument shows that a cycle in the Hasse graph makes the local stochastic cone non-simplicial, which obstructs the existence of the directed family of deflations required for an RB-domain. For the converse, assuming all stochastic cones are simplicial, one must construct a directed family of deflations with finite image approximating the identity. This could be done by projecting onto faces of the probability simplex corresponding to down-sets of P, using the tree structure implied by the simplicial cone condition.
directions.title: Simplicial Stochastic Cone Characterization of RB-Domains in Probabilistic Powerdomains

directions.description: For any full-dimensional convex polytope P in R^d, the cap-volume function V(H) = vol(P ∩ H⁺), mapping an oriented hyperplane H to the volume of the cap it cuts from P, is piecewise polynomial of degree exactly d on each full-dimensional cell of the arrangement induced by the vertices of P in the dual space of oriented hyperplanes. This strengthens the paper's key observation that V is piecewise rational to the sharper claim that it is piecewise polynomial, with the degree bound d arising from the fact that cap vertices on the hyperplane vary linearly in the hyperplane parameters while simplex volumes are degree-d polynomials in vertex coordinates.

directions.proof_strategy: Fix a full-dimensional cell C of the arrangement in the dual space where the combinatorial type of the cap P ∩ H⁺ is constant. Within C, the vertices of the cap are either original vertices of P (constant) or intersection points of edges of P with H. Show that these intersection points vary linearly in the hyperplane parameters on C. Triangulate the cap into simplices; each simplex volume is a degree-d polynomial in its vertex coordinates. Since each vertex is either constant or linear in the hyperplane parameters, each simplex volume is a degree-d polynomial in the hyperplane parameters on C. Summing over simplices yields a degree-d polynomial for the total cap volume on C. Genericity arguments show the degree is exactly d, not less.
directions.title: Piecewise Polynomial Cap-Volume Conjecture for Convex Polytopes

directions.description: The Giampietro-Darmon factorization formula for the norm of $p$-adic cross-ratios of CM points on Atkin-Lehner quotients of Shimura curves, currently proven only for genus 0 quotients, holds unconditionally for all squarefree $N > 1$ with an even number of prime factors. For quotients of higher genus, the infinite product of $p$-adic cross-ratios factors into a product of local intersection multiplicities of the corresponding Heegner divisors, up to a global obstruction given by the Néron-Tate height pairing on the Jacobian.

The factorization formula for the norm of the p-adic cross-ratio infinite product of CM points on the Shimura curve X_N holds if the Atkin-Lehner quotient X_N / w_p has genus 0. This extends the original Giampietro-Darmon conjecture, which required the Shimura curve X_N itself to have genus 0 (a condition only satisfied for N in {6, 10, 22}).

directions.description: The cyclotomic matrix $A_k(\chi) = [G_N(\chi^{ki+kj})]$ involving Gauss sums over $\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}$ (where $N=p^m$ and $n=\varphi(N)/k$) can be decomposed as the matrix product $W D W^T$, where $W$ is the $n \times n$ discrete Fourier transform matrix with entries $W_{i,a} = \omega^{ai}$ ($\omega$ being a primitive $n$-th root of unity) and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of the $n$ Gauss periods $\eta_a$ corresponding to the $k$-th power residue cyclotomic cosets.

Express $\chi^{k(i+j)}(x)$ as $\omega^{a(i+j)}$ for $x \in C_a$, pulling the root of unity out of the sum to yield $\sum_{a=0}^{n-1} \omega^{a(i+j)} \eta_a$, which directly translates to the matrix factorization $A_k(\chi) = W D W^T$.

directions.description: Every symmetric edge polytope of dimension at most 35 has a γ-positive Ehrhart h*-polynomial. Equivalently, 36 is the minimum dimension of a symmetric edge polytope whose Ehrhart h*-polynomial fails to be γ-positive. This would sharpen the paper's existence result by establishing the exact threshold, confirming that no smaller counterexamples to the Ohsugi–Tsuchiya conjecture exist.

directions.title: Dimension Threshold for Gamma-Positivity of Symmetric Edge Polytopes

Establish structural properties of graphs with non-positive curvature edges, and demonstrate that exceeding the edge threshold T(n) precludes the existence of such subgraphs, thereby forcing all edge curvatures to be strictly positive.

directions.description: For the fixed genus chord swap Markov chain on chord diagrams with n chords and genus g, the spectral gap γ_{n,g} satisfies γ_{n,g} = Θ(n^{-3}) when g is fixed and n → ∞. This sharpens the paper's polynomial lower bound to a precise exponent and matches the n^{-3} scaling observed in related swap chains on perfect matchings.

Then establish the O(n^{-3}) upper bound on the spectral gap via comparison with the random transposition walk on matchings, and prove the Ω(n^{-3}) lower bound by constructing a canonical path argument with congestion bounded by O(n^3), extending the paper's coupling/canonical-path techniques.
directions.title: Tight spectral gap exponent for the fixed-genus chord swap chain

directions.description: Every symmetric r-coloring of the Hales-Jewett cube [t]^n — one invariant under all coordinate permutations of the word — is a one-weight coloring: there exist integer weights w_1, ..., w_t such that the color of a word x ∈ [t]^n depends only on the weighted sum ∑_i w_{x_i}. Conversely, every one-weight coloring is symmetric. This equivalence reduces the symmetric lower-bound problem for Hales-Jewett numbers to the d=1 case of Gallai's theorem on homothetic copies of a t-point set in Z.
domain_bridges: Integer-weighted letter sums as complete invariants

For the converse, given a symmetric coloring c, construct the radix weight by examining how c distinguishes words that differ only in letter substitution: define w_j - w_1 as the minimal coordinate substitution that changes the color class when swapping a letter 1 for letter j in a fixed position. Show that the orbit of any word under coordinate permutations is determined by its letter-count vector, and that c factors through the weighted sum because symmetry forces c to depend only on the letter-count, which the radix weight encodes injectively modulo the kernel of c. The key combinatorial lemma is that the color partition of Z induced by the weighted sum is well-defined and independent of the choice of representative word.
directions.title: Symmetric Colorings of Hales-Jewett Cubes Coincide with One-Weight Colorings

directions.description: For all finite graphs F and G, there exists an oddomorphism from F to G if and only if G is a split-off minor of F. The forward direction is established in the paper; the converse remains open.

For the converse, attempt to construct an oddomorphism from F to G given that G is a split-off minor of F, by reversing each split-off minor operation step and verifying parity conditions on homomorphism counts are preserved. A counterexample search via CFI-type constructions could also be pursued.

directions.description: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let F ∈ k[x₁,…,x_d] be irreducible. Then F = H(f₁(x₁)+⋯+f_d(x_d)) for some H ∈ k[t] with deg(H) ≥ 2 and fᵢ ∈ k[t] if and only if there exist rational functions α₁,ⱼ ∈ k(xⱼ), α₂,ᵢ ∈ k(xᵢ), and G ∈ k(x₁,…,x_d) such that for every i ∈ {1,…,d}: ∂F/∂xᵢ ≡ G · α₂,ᵢ(xᵢ) · ∏_{j≠i} α₁,ⱼ(xⱼ) (mod ⟨F⟩), where crucially the α₁,ⱼ factors are independent of i. This is the algebraic analogue of Theorem 2.3, replacing analytic isomorphisms with rational function substitutions and local neighborhoods with Zariski-open conditions.

directions.description: For any prime power q and integers 2 ≤ m ≤ n, the multilinear forms Cayley graph Γ(F_q^{2×m×n}) generated by rank-one tensors has exactly m+1 distinct eigenvalues, in one-to-one correspondence with the possible ranks r ∈ {0, 1, ..., m} of m×n matrices over F_q. This generalizes the complete spectrum computation for 2×3×3 tensors established in the paper, where m=3 yields 4 distinct eigenvalues determined by the rank distribution of 3×3 matrices. Despite the graph failing to be distance-regular for order-3 tensors, the spectral structure for the 2×m×n format remains governed entirely by the rank-metric code distribution.

directions.proof_strategy: Extend the recursive spectral analysis from the 2×3×3 case to general 2×m×n format by decomposing the character sum over rank-one tensors according to the rank profile of the corresponding m×n matrix slice, leveraging the established connection between tensor subspace intersections with the Segre variety and the rank distribution of the associated rank-metric codes. The key step is showing that characters indexed by tensors whose m×n slices have equal rank produce identical eigenvalues, yielding exactly m+1 distinct spectral values.
directions.title: Distinct Eigenvalue Count for 2×m×n Multilinear Forms Cayley Graphs

directions.description: For any simple graph G with n vertices and m edges, and for any 1 ≤ k ≤ n-1, the sum of the k largest Laplacian eigenvalues s_k(G) equals m + binom(k+1, 2) if and only if G is a threshold graph with clique number k+1.

Show that equality in Brouwer's bound implies equality in Grone-Merris-Bai, forcing the degree sequence to match the Laplacian eigenvalue sequence. Use the characterization of threshold graphs via their degree sequences and the specific sum m + binom(k+1, 2) to conclude that G must be a threshold graph with clique number k+1.

Specifically, the alternating Hurwitz kernel K_E^{2n+1}(α, x) := ½ζ_E(2n+1, x) + Σ_{m=1}^∞ m^{-2n-1}/(e^{2αm} + 1) obeys: α^{-n}·K_E^{2n+1}(α, x) − (−β)^{-n}·K_E^{2n+1}(β, 1−x) = 2^{2n} Σ_{k=0}^{n+1} (−1)^{k−1} E_{2k}(x) B_{2n−2k+2} / ((2k)!(2n−2k+2)!) · α^{n−k+1} β^k, where E_{2k}(x) are Euler polynomials and B_{2k} are Bernoulli numbers. This replaces the Bernoulli numbers B_{2k} in Ramanujan's original identity with Euler polynomials E_{2k}(x), reflecting the alternating (sign-twisted) structure.

    = (2 : ℝ)^(2*n) * ∑ k in Finset.range (n + 2),
        ((-1 : ℝ)^(k - 1) * eulerPoly (2*k) x * bernoulli (2*n - 2*k + 2))
        / ((2*k).factorial * (2*n - 2*k + 2).factorial) * α^(n - k + 1) * β^k :=

directions.description: For every doubly regular tournament on n vertices (where n ≡ 3 mod 4 and n ≥ 3), the metric dimension β(G) is at most ⌈3·log₂(n)⌉. This provides an explicit constant in the O(log n) bound established for related families in the paper, extending the probabilistic method of Babai to the directed tournament setting with a constructive resolvability guarantee.

Use the strong regularity properties to bound this probability below 1/n², then take a union bound over all pairs. The key structural lemma is that in a doubly regular tournament, for any distinct u,v, the set {s : d(s,u) ≠ d(s,v)} has size at least n/3, giving each sample at least a 1/3 chance of distinguishing u from v.

directions.description: The paper proves that for k ≥ 3 and sufficiently large n, the maximum number of points in an n × n grid with no k+1 collinear points equals kn. This conjecture asserts that 'sufficiently large' can be replaced by the explicit threshold n ≥ k. Note that for n ≤ k the whole grid has no k+1 collinear points so f_k(n) = n², and for n = k we get f_k(k) = k² = k·k, making n ≥ k the natural boundary. The conjecture predicts that for all k ≥ 3 and n ≥ k, the trivial upper bound kn is always achievable.

To push 'sufficiently large n' down to n ≥ k, one would need to make each step effective with explicit bounds. The hypergraph matching step likely requires the most careful analysis for small n. A computer-verified case analysis for small n (up to some explicit bound) combined with the asymptotic argument for larger n could work. The key is determining whether the o(n) deletion/swinging losses can be controlled when n is close to k.

directions.description: For every integer n ≥ 3, there exists a constant c_n > 0 such that for every positive integer m, the density of primitive maximal binary forms of degree n (ordered by height) that simultaneously fail the integral Hasse principle for all F(x,y) = h with 1 ≤ h ≤ m is at least c_n / m^{n−2}. This refines the paper's result that this density is merely positive for each fixed m, conjecturing an explicit polynomial decay rate in m governed by the degree.

    liminf (fun X => N_fail X m / N X) ≥ c / m ^ (n - 2)

This requires uniform estimates on the density of forms with prescribed local behavior at finitely many primes, combined with the sieving framework already present in the paper.

The case m=3 appears in the paper as a key lemma simplifying the Bogart–Longyear formula for L_{3,n}, and the case m=2 is the classical Chu–Vandermonde identity. The general form underpins Gessel's formula for m-row Latin rectangles and its 3D rook polynomial generalization.

directions.description: For every d ≥ 3, the supremum of normalized surface measures of zero-sum-free measurable subsets of the unit sphere S^{d-1} in ℝ^d equals exactly 1/2. Equivalently, every measurable zero-sum-free A ⊆ S^{d-1} satisfies σ_{d-1}(A) ≤ 1/2, with equality achieved (only) by open hemispheres. The paper establishes the asymptotic bound m_d ≤ 1/2 + O(1/d), but the exact value m_d = 1/2 remains open.

This conjecture proposes that the implicit constant in the upper bound can be taken to be 2, i.e., f(a,k) ≤ 2a + 2k + ⌈2ak / log(k+2)⌉ for all integers a,k ≥ 2. This would make the asymptotic result fully explicit and represents a natural strengthening of the paper's greedy-packing upper bound argument.

This is the main theorem (Theorem 1.1) of the paper. Formalizing it requires developing the theories of generic representations of GL_r over p-adic fields, both integral-representation (Jacquet–Shalika) and Langlands–Shahidi constructions of L- and ε-factors, and the local functional equation for the Jacquet–Shalika exterior square integrals.

directions.description: The paper establishes a directed analogue of the Bonnet-Myers theorem: for a strongly connected, r-regular simple digraph G with in-curvature κ⁻(v) ≥ κ₀ > 0 at every vertex, the directed diameter is bounded above by 2r/κ₀. The natural rigidity conjecture is that equality in this bound forces G to be a directed cycle. Specifically, if G is a strongly connected, r-regular simple digraph with in-curvature κ⁻(v) ≥ κ₀ > 0 for all v, and the directed diameter satisfies ⟶diam(G) = 2r/κ₀, then G is isomorphic to a directed cycle C_n (where n = 2r/κ₀ + 1). This mirrors Obata's rigidity theorem for the classical Lichnerowicz inequality and would complete the directed Bonnet-Myers picture.

(5) The key technical step is proving that any deviation from the directed cycle structure strictly increases the effective resistance / decreases curvature below κ₀, contradicting the equality assumption.

This is the core quantitative claim of the paper, establishing that the Minkowski grid construction yields a polynomial improvement over the trivial n bound for distance multiplicity, thereby disproving Erdős's unit distance conjecture.

directions.description: For every integer d ≥ 2, if p ∈ ℂ[s] is a nonzero balanced polynomial (satisfying p(s) = ω·conj(p(−conj(s))) for some |ω| = 1) whose zeros all lie in the region Ω_d = {a+ib : a² − b²/(d−1) ≤ d/4}, then the centered binomial sample B_d[p](z) = Σ_{j=0}^{d} C(d,j)·p(j−d/2)·z^j has all its zeros on the unit circle. Furthermore, Ω_d is the maximal reflection-invariant set with this property: for any reflection-invariant S ⊋ Ω_d, there exists a balanced polynomial with zeros in S whose binomial sample has a zero off the unit circle. This is the polynomial case of the paper's main sampling theorem, which then drives the derivative-period-polynomial unit-circle theorem for L-functions of newforms.
domain_bridges: Sampling theory → Zero distribution of L-functions

directions.description: The infimum μ₂ over all infinite sequences of radial cuts of the ratio between the maximum and minimum portion (adjacent pair of slices) sizes equals 1+ρ, where ρ is the unique real root of ρ²+ρ³=1 in (0,1). The paper proves μ₂ ≤ 1+ρ ≈ 1.75488 and Korsky proved μ₂ ≥ 5/3 ≈ 1.66667, but the exact value remains open.

Equivalently, this is exactly the range where PF_t(G) is shellable and sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. For t ≤ 2n_{m-1} - 2, the complex fails to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay.

directions.description: The paper proves that the count N(x) of odd integers up to x not representable as p+2^a+2^b is at least x * exp(-(4+η) * (logloglogx / loglogx) * logx). This conjecture posits that the constant 4 in the exponent is an artifact of the Fermat number construction and can be replaced by any arbitrarily small epsilon > 0, yielding a lower bound of x * exp(-ε * (logloglogx / loglogx) * logx). This would substantially bridge the gap to Erdős's grand challenge conjecture that N(x) > c_0 * x for some constant c_0 > 0.

This conjecture states that this complicated product simplifies to a product of binomial coefficients: T_n = ∏_{k=1}^n (3k-1 choose k). This is a precise, falsifiable identity that can be checked for small n and would provide a much simpler closed form.

directions.description: For every doubly regular tournament T on n vertices (where n ≡ 3 mod 4, n ≥ 3), the metric dimension β(T) ≤ 2⌈log₂ n⌉. This extends the paper's O(log n) bound proven for certain doubly regular team tournaments to the classical and well-studied family of doubly regular tournaments, which are regular tournaments with parameters (n, (n-1)/2, (n-3)/4). The conjecture posits an explicit constant of 2, making it directly falsifiable by computing metric dimensions of small doubly regular tournaments (n = 3, 7, 11, 19, ...) and checking against the bound.

Compute the probability that two distinct vertices u, v receive the same distance vector from the sampled set. Use the strong regularity properties of doubly regular tournaments—specifically that every pair of vertices has exactly (n-3)/4 common out-neighbours—to bound the collision probability per pair by 1/2^k. Apply a union bound over all n(n-1)/2 pairs, choosing k so that the union bound is < 1, yielding a resolving set of size at most 2⌈log₂ n⌉.

This would unify the trivial case ($n \le k$, where $f_k(n) = n^2$) and the asymptotic regime.

The generalization connects directly to Gessel's framework through multisymmetric function generating series.
