directions.description: Bach's chorales are the gold standard of Western harmony. But what if we could MEASURE the harmonic complexity using topology? Encode each chord as a point in a 12-dimensional space (one dimension per pitch class). A sequence of chords traces a path in this space. Compute the persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a Bach chorale. Conjecture: Bach's chorales have persistent H_1 (1-dimensional cycles) that survive across a wide range of scales, indicating circular harmonic motion (the circle of fifths). In contrast, random chord sequences have H_1 bars that die quickly. The longest H_1 bar in a Bach chorale corresponds to the circle of fifths — the fundamental harmonic cycle. Pop music has shorter H_1 bars (less complex harmonic cycles). Atonal music has no persistent H_1 (no harmonic cycles). Test: compute persistent homology barcodes for 100 Bach chorales, 100 pop songs, and 100 atonal pieces. Verify: Bach has H_1 bars of length > 0.5 (in normalized pitch-class space), pop has bars of length 0.2-0.5, atonal has no persistent H_1. Impact: the topology of music IS its harmonic structure. Bach's genius is literally topological — his music has longer harmonic cycles.
directions.proof_strategy: Encode each chord as a binary vector in {0,1}^12 (pitch class set). Map to R^12 using the Fourier transform: each pitch class k maps to e^{2*pi*i*k/12}, giving a point on the unit circle. A chord maps to the sum of its pitch class vectors, normalized. Compute persistent homology of the point cloud of all chords in a piece using Vietoris-Rips complexes. For Bach: the circle of fifths creates a persistent H_1 cycle because chord progressions follow the circle (C -> G -> D -> A -> E -> B -> F# -> C# -> G# -> D# -> A# -> F -> C). This cycle survives across multiple scales. For pop: the cycle is shorter (typically I -> V -> vi -> IV -> I, a 4-chord loop). For atonal: no persistent cycle. Compute: Rips filtration for epsilon = 0.1, 0.2, ..., 1.0. Measure H_1 bar lengths. Test: verify Bach H_1 bars > 0.5, pop H_1 bars 0.2-0.5, atonal H_1 bars < 0.2.
directions.title: Persistent Homology of Musical Harmony: The Topology of Bach

directions.description: The Galois group of a random polynomial over Q is S_n with probability 1. This is the Hilbert irreducibility theorem in probabilistic form. But what about random polynomials over finite fields? For f in F_p[x] of degree n chosen uniformly at random, the Galois group is S_n with probability approaching 1 as p grows. Conjecture: the probability that Gal(f) is NOT S_n is O(p^{-1/2}) for fixed n, and the exceptional cases concentrate at polynomials with discriminant zero or small Galois groups. More precisely, P(Gal(f) != S_n) = c_n / sqrt(p) + O(1/p) where c_n depends only on n. For n=2: P(Gal(f) != S_2) = P(discriminant = 0) = 1/p. For n=3: P(Gal(f) != S_3) = P(f has a rational root) = 3/p + O(1/p^2). Test: enumerate all monic polynomials of degree n over F_p for small p and n, compute Galois groups, verify P(Gal != S_n) ~ c_n / sqrt(p). Impact: random polynomials have maximal Galois groups — algebraic randomness is generic.
directions.proof_strategy: For a random monic polynomial f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + ... + a_0 over F_p, the Galois group is a subgroup of S_n. Compute P(Gal(f) = S_n) by counting. For n=2: Gal(f) = S_2 unless discriminant = a_1^2 - 4*a_0 = 0, which happens for p choices of a_1 (each gives one a_0), so P = 1 - p/p^2 = 1 - 1/p. For n=3: Gal(f) != S_3 iff f has a rational root (3 choices of root, each determines f) or Gal = A_3 (discriminant is a square). Count both cases. For general n: use the fact that random permutations have cycle structure converging to the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution. The Galois group is S_n unless there is an 'obvious' factorization, which happens with probability O(1/p). Test: implement in Lean 4 + Python. For p=2..100 and n=2..6, enumerate all monic polynomials, compute factorizations, estimate P(Gal != S_n).
directions.title: Stochastic Galois Theory: Random Permutations Have Generic Galois Groups

directions.description: Sudoku is a constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). Random Sudoku instances exhibit a phase transition: for n^2 x n^2 grids, the probability of having a solution drops from ~1 to ~0 around a critical density of pre-filled cells. Conjecture: the phase transition occurs at density d_c(n) = (n^2 - 1) / n^2, independent of the specific constraint structure. For standard 9x9 Sudoku (n=3): d_c = 8/9 ≈ 0.889. For 4x4 Sudoku (n=2): d_c = 3/4 = 0.75. For 16x16 (n=4): d_c = 15/16 ≈ 0.9375. The 'hardness' of random Sudoku peaks at the phase transition: instances with density near d_c take exponentially longer to solve than easy (low density) or trivial (high density) instances. Conjecture: the computational hardness of Sudoku at the phase transition is O(exp(n^2)) for backtracking algorithms, matching the theoretical prediction for CSPs at criticality. Test: generate random Sudoku instances at varying densities, measure solver time, and verify the phase transition at d_c. Impact: Sudoku hardness is not about 9x9 grids — it is about the phase transition structure of constraint satisfaction.
directions.proof_strategy: Define random Sudoku(G, d) as a G x G grid with d * G^2 cells pre-filled uniformly at random, subject to the constraint that the pre-filled cells are consistent (no two same numbers in the same row/column/box). For n^2 x n^2 grids: G = n^2. The density d = (# pre-filled) / G^2. Phase transition: P(solvable) as a function of d. For n=2 (4x4): d_c = 3/4. For n=3 (9x9): d_c = 8/9. Theoretical basis: the number of solutions of an empty G x G grid is S(G). Adding a constraint reduces the solution count by approximately S(G)/G. At density d, the number of solutions is approximately S(G) * (1 - 1/G)^{d*G^2} ≈ S(G) * exp(-d*G). This is > 0 when d < (ln S(G))/G ≈ (G-1)/G = d_c. Hardness: at density d near d_c, the expected number of backtracks is exp(O(G)). Test: generate 10000 random Sudoku instances at each density from 0.5 to 0.99, solve with backtracking, measure time, verify phase transition at d_c.
directions.title: The P vs NP of Sudoku: Phase Transitions in Constraint Satisfaction

directions.description: Anyon braiding in topological quantum computing gives unitary matrices from the braid group B_n. The Jones representation rho_k: B_n -> U((k-1)(n-1)+1) at root of unity e^{2*pi*i/k} is conjectured to be universal for quantum computation when k >= 3 and n >= 4. Conjecture: the set of all braids in B_4 under the Jones representation at k=5 generates a dense subgroup of SU(3). More precisely, the image rho_5(B_4) is an infinite subgroup of SU(3) that is not contained in any proper closed subgroup. This means that topological quantum computing with Fibonacci anyons (k=5) is universal: any unitary in SU(3) can be approximated to arbitrary precision by braiding 4 anyons. The key: the Jones representation at k=5 gives 3x3 matrices, and the braid generators sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 generate a dense subgroup of SU(3). Test: compute the Jones representation at k=5 for B_4, verify that sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 has infinite order, and check that the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 is dense in SU(3) by the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. Impact: braiding anyons is universal for quantum computation. The braid group B_4 at k=5 is a quantum gate set.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the braid group B_n = <sigma_1, ..., sigma_{n-1} | sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}>. The Jones representation at root of unity q = e^{2*pi*i/k}: for k=5, q = e^{2*pi*i/5}, the representation rho_5: B_4 -> SU(3). Compute the matrices: sigma_1 = rho_5(sigma_1), sigma_2 = rho_5(sigma_2), sigma_3 = rho_5(sigma_3). These are 3x3 unitary matrices. Verify: (1) sigma_i * sigma_j = sigma_j * sigma_i for |i-j| > 1, (2) sigma_i * sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i = sigma_{i+1} * sigma_i * sigma_{i+1}. Check density: compute sigma_1 * sigma_2 * sigma_3 and verify it has infinite order (the trace is not a root of unity). Apply the Solovay-Kitaev theorem: if the group generated by sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 contains a non-commuting pair and is infinite, then it is dense in SU(3). Test: implement in Python using numpy, compute the Jones representation matrices, verify the braid relations, and check density by approximating random SU(3) matrices.
directions.title: Topological Quantum Compiling: Braid Groups as Universal Gates

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers No form a proper class containing all real numbers, all ordinal numbers, and all infinitesimals. Every real number r has a surreal representation r = {r - 1 | r + 1}. Every ordinal alpha has a surreal representation alpha = {alpha |}. Every infinitesimal epsilon = {0 | 1, 1/2, 1/4, ...}. The surreal numbers form a field (in fact, a real-closed field). Conjecture: the subfield of surreals born by day omega (the set of surreals with finite birthdays) is isomorphic to the field of real algebraic numbers extended with all dyadic rationals. More precisely: No_{omega} = Q[2^{-n} : n in N] (the rationals extended with all dyadic rationals). The subfield born by day omega^2 contains all real numbers that are algebraic over the dyadic rationals, plus all infinitesimals that are algebraic over the reals. Conjecture: No_{omega^2} = R(x) where x is the smallest positive infinitesimal. Test: compute the field structure of surreals born by day omega and verify the isomorphism with the dyadic rationals. Impact: the surreal number hierarchy encodes the constructive hierarchy of real number fields — each birthday level adds exactly the algebraic closures needed.
directions.proof_strategy: Define No_alpha = {surreals with birthday < alpha}. No_0 = empty. No_1 = {0} = {{|}}. No_2 = {-1, 0, 1} (three surreals). No_3 = {-2, -1/2, -1, -1/4, 0, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2} (but actually No_3 has 7 surreals). By day omega: No_omega = all dyadic rationals m/2^n for m in Z, n in N. This is a field: the dyadic rationals are closed under +, -, *, / (for nonzero). Proof: m/2^n + k/2^l = (m*2^l + k*2^n)/2^{n+l} which is dyadic. Product: (m/2^n)(k/2^l) = mk/2^{n+l}. Reciprocal: 1/(m/2^n) = 2^n/m which is rational (not always dyadic). Wait: 1/3 is not dyadic. So No_omega is not closed under reciprocals of odd denominators. Correction: No_omega is the ring of dyadic rationals, not a field. The field of fractions is Q (all rationals). Conjecture revised: the field of fractions of No_omega is Q, the rationals. No_{omega^2} includes all real numbers that can be constructed by day omega^2, which includes all real algebraic numbers (since each algebraic number has a finite Dedekind cut representation). Test: enumerate surreals by birthday and verify field closure.
directions.title: The Arithmetic of Games: Surreal Numbers as Number Fields

directions.description: The Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum error-correcting codes are constructed from classical linear codes C_1, C_2 with C_2 perp subset C_1. The CSS code encodes dim(C_1) - dim(C_2) logical qubits. This is exactly the definition of a cohomology group: H^1(C_1, C_2) = C_1 / C_2. Conjecture: every CSS code is equivalent to a cohomology computation on a simplicial complex, and vice versa. Specifically, given a simplicial complex K, the CSS code with C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries) encodes dim(H_1(K, F_2)) logical qubits with distance d = min(length of shortest non-trivial cycle, length of shortest non-trivial cocycle). This is the homological quantum error-correcting code HQECC(K). The distance d equals the systole of K (the length of the shortest non-contractible cycle). Conjecture: for the hypercube Q_n (n-dimensional cube graph), the HQECC encodes 1 qubit with distance d = 2^{n/2} (achieving the quantum Singleton bound). Test: construct HQECC for Q_4, Q_6, Q_8 and verify the parameters. Impact: quantum error correction is cohomology. Every simplicial complex gives a quantum code, and the code parameters are topological invariants.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the CSS construction: given F_2-linear codes C_2 perp subset C_1 subset F_2^n, the CSS code is the subspace spanned by {|v + C_2> : v in C_1}. This encodes k = dim(C_1/C_2) = dim(H^1) logical qubits. Define HQECC(K): for a simplicial complex K, let C_1 = Z_1(K, F_2) (1-cycles mod F_2) and C_2 = B_1(K, F_2) (1-boundaries). Then H_1(K, F_2) = Z_1/B_1 is the first homology. The CSS code with these C_1, C_2 encodes dim(H_1) qubits. Distance: d_X = min weight of non-trivial cycle in Z_1 \ B_1, d_Z = min weight of non-trivial cocycle. The code distance d = min(d_X, d_Z). For hypercube Q_n: H_1(Q_n, F_2) = F_2^{n choose 2} (since Q_n has n choose 2 independent 1-cycles). Wait, that's for n >= 3. Actually Q_n is bipartite, so H_1 has dimension (n choose 2). The systole of Q_n is 4 (the shortest cycle). So d = min(4, something). Need to compute d_Z: the shortest non-trivial cocycle. For Q_n, d_Z = 2^{n/2} by the MacWilliams identity. Test: construct CSS codes from simplicial complexes, compute parameters [[n, k, d]].
directions.title: Quantum Error Correction from Homological Algebra: CSS Codes as Cohomology

# Future Directions: The Geometry and Universal Structure of Surprise

This cycle established two complementary pillars. First, *surprise* — the gap between
the most conservative and most divergent resolution of a setup — is a genuine
geometric invariant equal to the diameter of the resolution configuration
(nonnegative, vanishing exactly on constant setups, monotone under refinement, and
attained). Second, when a *canonical* (terminal) resolution exists, it is unique in the
strongest possible sense: up to a unique, coherent isomorphism, and it is rigid. The
following conjectures push both pillars further.

## 1. Surprise as a genuine metric diameter in higher dimensions

**Conjecture.** For a finite configuration of resolutions embedded in a Euclidean space
of any dimension, the natural surprise invariant equals the metric diameter of the
configuration's convex hull, and it remains monotone under enrichment and subadditive
under overlays of setups.

**The key insight is** that the one-dimensional identity "surprise = range = greatest
pairwise distance" is not special to the line: it is a shadow of the general fact that
the extreme spread of a compact configuration is realised on its boundary.

**Why now?** The one-dimensional case is fully settled here with an attained diameter
characterisation, giving an exact template — extremal witnesses plus a uniform bound —
that generalises verbatim once "endpoints" are replaced by "hull vertices."

## 2. A vanishing dichotomy separating puns from absurdism

**Conjecture.** The surprise invariant admits a sharp threshold: below it, every setup
is equivalent (after normalisation) to a near-constant configuration; above it, setups
necessarily contain two resolutions in "different categories" that no refinement can
reconcile.

**The key insight is** that the zero-surprise characterisation is not merely a boundary
case but the base of a stratification: distance from the constant locus measures how
far a setup has escaped its expected resolution.

**Why now?** We have proven the exact vanishing locus (surprise `0` iff all resolutions
coincide) and that surprise is monotone; a stratification by surprise value is the
immediate next quantitative refinement.

## 3. Universal resolutions as limits of refinement chains

**Conjecture.** Every setup whose resolutions form a directed refinement system admits a
universal resolution, obtained as the colimit of the refinement chain, and this colimit
is automatically rigid.

**The key insight is** that terminality — proven here to force unique, coherent,
rigidity-witnessing structure — is exactly the property a well-behaved colimit inherits,
so existence of the canonical resolution reduces to directedness of refinements.

**Why now?** The abstract uniqueness and rigidity of terminal resolutions are already in
hand; the only missing ingredient for a general existence theorem is a construction, and
directed colimits supply the standard one.

## 4. Sharp stability of surprise under perturbation

**Status.** The basic stability estimate is now settled: perturbing every resolution of
a setup by at most `ε` changes its surprise by at most `2ε`. This confirms that surprise
is a robust invariant — small changes in how each resolution is read cannot produce a
large change in humor.

**Conjecture (next step).** The factor `2` is optimal, and more is true: surprise is a
contraction under any reinterpretation that is itself a contraction of the resolution
axis, and the estimate composes — a chain of `k` perturbations of sizes `ε₁, …, ε_k`
moves surprise by at most `2(ε₁ + ⋯ + ε_k)`, with equality achieved on suitably
"stretched" two-point setups.

**The key insight is** that surprise is built from two extremal selectors, each of which
moves by at most the perturbation size, so their difference is controlled — and that the
worst case is realised precisely when the two extremes are pushed apart in opposite
directions, which pins down the sharp constant.

**Why now?** The extremal (`IsGreatest`/`IsLeast`) characterisations of the two canonical
resolutions, together with the just-established `2ε` stability bound, are exactly the
ingredients needed to identify the extremal configurations that make the constant sharp.

directions.description: Sorting a list of n elements reduces the entropy from log(n!) bits to 0 bits, doing thermodynamic work W = kT * log(n!) in the process. But this is only true if sorting is irreversible — if the sorted list uniquely determines the input, then sorting is reversible and does no thermodynamic work. The key insight: comparison-based sorting makes irreversible comparisons (you learn a < b but discard the possibility a > b), and each comparison reduces entropy by at most 1 bit. So n*log(n) comparisons reduce entropy by at most n*log(n) bits, which matches log(n!) ~ n*log(n) bits. Conjecture: the minimum thermodynamic work of sorting n elements is W_min = kT * log(n!), and this work is achieved by optimal comparison-based sorting algorithms (merge sort, heapsort). Sub-optimal algorithms (bubble sort: n^2 comparisons) do more thermodynamic work than necessary: W_bubble = kT * n^2, wasting kT * (n^2 - n*log(n)) bits of entropy reduction. Conjecture: any sorting algorithm that makes C(n) comparisons does thermodynamic work proportional to C(n) * kT, and the optimal work is W_min = kT * n*log(n) (Stirling's approximation). Test: simulate sorting algorithms with entropy bookkeeping, verify W = kT * log(n!) for merge sort and W = kT * n^2 for bubble sort. Impact: sorting is a thermodynamic process. The n*log(n) lower bound is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the entropy of a permutation: S(pi) = -sum_i p_i * log(p_i) where pi is a permutation of n elements. Initially, all n! permutations are equally likely, so S_initial = log(n!) bits. After sorting, only one permutation (the identity) is possible, so S_final = 0. The thermodynamic work is W = kT * (S_initial - S_final) = kT * log(n!). Each comparison in a sorting algorithm reduces entropy by at most 1 bit: comparing a and b tells you one bit (whether a < b or a > b), reducing the number of possible permutations by a factor of at most 2. So C comparisons reduce entropy by at most C bits. For optimal sorting: C(n) = n*log(n) (merge sort), so W = kT * n*log(n) ≈ kT * log(n!) (by Stirling). For bubble sort: C(n) = n^2/2, so W = kT * n^2/2 >> kT * log(n!). The excess work is kT * (n^2/2 - n*log(n)), which is thermodynamic waste. Test: implement merge sort and bubble sort with entropy counters, verify entropy reduction per comparison.
directions.title: The Thermodynamics of Sorting: Entropy and Computational Work

# Future Directions — Emotional Chromatic Number of Social Networks

The emotional chromatic number `emoChrom G = min { k ≥ 3 : G is k-colorable }` is the smallest
number of emotion categories (at least three) needed to assign emotions to people so that no two
friends share one. The current cycle establishes `emoChrom(K_n) = max(n, 3)`, `emoChrom(C_n) = 3`
for `n ≥ 3`, the six-emotion window `3 ≤ emoChrom ≤ 6` for 6-colorable networks, and refutes the
folklore "bipartite root at k = 2." The following conjectures push the invariant further.

## 1. The emotional floor is the only correction: `emoChrom = max(χ, 3)`

**Conjecture.** For every finite graph `G`, `emoChrom G = max(χ(G), 3)`, so the emotional chromatic
number is determined by the ordinary chromatic number and a universal floor.

**The key insight is** that colorability is monotone in the number of colors, so the set of admissible
emotion counts is an interval `[max(χ, 3), ∞)` whose least element is `max(χ, 3)`; the emotional
constraint contributes exactly one thing — the floor at three.

**Why now?** The clique and cycle computations already exhibit both regimes (`χ ≥ 3` cliques track
`χ`, while `χ = 2` bipartite graphs are lifted to `3`), so a single uniform identity is the natural
consolidation and would make every downstream emotional statistic a corollary of chromatic theory.

## 2. Emotional monotonicity under friendship growth

**Conjecture.** Adding a friendship (an edge) to a social network can raise the emotional chromatic
number by at most one, and removing one can lower it by at most one; consequently networks that
differ in a single friendship have emotional chromatic numbers differing by at most one.

**The key insight is** that a proper coloring of the larger graph restricts to the smaller one, while
a coloring of the smaller graph extends across a new edge after recoloring at most one endpoint, so
the invariant is 1-Lipschitz with respect to edge edits.

**Why now?** Deletion–contraction (already formalized for the chromatic polynomial in this catalog)
gives exact control of how coloring counts change under edge edits; lifting that control from counts
to the floored minimum `emoChrom` is the immediate next step.

## 3. Sparse networks stay inside the six-emotion window

**Conjecture.** Every social network in which each person has at most five friends satisfies
`emoChrom G ≤ 6`; more generally, bounded-degree networks have emotional chromatic number bounded by
one more than the maximum number of friends, capped below by three.

**The key insight is** that a greedy assignment, processing people one at a time, always finds a free
emotion whenever the number of already-colored friends is below the palette size, so `deg_max + 1`
emotions always suffice.

**Why now?** Real friendship networks are overwhelmingly sparse, so a degree-based bound explains the
empirical observation that emotional chromatic numbers cluster in `[3, 6]`, turning the six-emotion
window from a hypothesis into a structural guarantee for realistic networks.

## 4. Planarity forces at most six emotions

**Conjecture.** Every social network that can be drawn without crossing friendships (a planar
network) has emotional chromatic number in `{3, 4}`, and never needs more than four emotions.

**The key insight is** that planar graphs are four-colorable, so the floor and the four-color bound
squeeze the invariant into a two-value range, independent of network size.

**Why now?** Many geographically embedded social networks are approximately planar, so a sharp
two-value classification would give an exact emotional taxonomy for an entire, practically relevant
family of networks.

## 5. The emotional floor detects triangle-free structure

**Conjecture.** Among triangle-free social networks, `emoChrom G = 3` precisely captures the
non-bipartite ones together with the trivial floor: a triangle-free network has emotional chromatic
number `3` iff it is either non-bipartite (contains an odd friendship cycle) or has at least one
friendship, and there exist triangle-free networks with arbitrarily large ordinary chromatic number
yet whose emotional profile is dominated by the floor only until χ overtakes it.

**The key insight is** that the emotional floor masks the fine distinction between χ = 2 and χ = 3,
so the invariant becomes a coarse odd-cycle detector until chromatic number climbs past three.

**Why now?** Triangle-free graphs with large chromatic number (Mycielski-type constructions) are a
classical source of surprises; testing how the emotional floor interacts with them probes exactly
where the invariant stops being a simple floor and starts tracking deep chromatic structure.
directions.title: The emotional chromatic number `emoChrom G = min { k ≥ 3 : G is k-colorable }` i

# Future Directions — The Topology of Arithmetic

This cycle established that the zero-dimensional persistent barcode of the prime
point cloud on the line is exactly the sequence of prime gaps, and that the twin
prime conjecture is the assertion that a length-`2` bar recurs forever.  The
following conjectures push the program further.

## 1. The gap-value spectrum is the set of barcode step-points

**Conjecture.** For the prime point cloud, the set of scales at which the number
of connected components strictly decreases equals the set of values attained by
the gap sequence, and each even number `2k` that occurs as a gap contributes a
positive-density family of bars of that exact death scale.

*The key insight is* that on a line the barcode is a lossless recording of the
gap multiset, so distributional questions about prime gaps (Polignac-type
statements) become questions about the multiplicity of individual bar lengths.

*Why now?* The single-linkage characterisation proved this cycle turns "how many
gaps equal `2k`" into "how many bars have death scale `2k`", making every result
on gap frequencies immediately a statement about barcode multiplicities.

## 2. A persistence-stability form of the average gap law

**Conjecture.** The empirical distribution of the first `N` finite `H_0` bar
lengths, rescaled by `log p_N`, converges to a fixed limiting profile; in
particular the mean bar length is asymptotic to `log p_N`.

*The key insight is* that the average bar length over the first `N` primes equals
`(p_N − p_1)/N`, a telescoping identity, so the prime number theorem controls the
first moment of the barcode directly.

*Why now?* With the barcode identified with the gap sequence, the mean-length
statement is exactly `(p_{N+1} − 2)/N → ` the average gap, and only the higher
moments and the shape of the limiting profile remain open.

## 3. Higher homology from the two-dimensional prime lattice

**Conjecture.** Embedding primes as the planar cloud `p_n ↦ (p_n, p_{n+1})` and
running the Rips filtration produces a first non-trivial `H_1` class whose birth
scale is governed by admissible gap patterns `(g_n, g_{n+1})`, and the shortest
persistent loop corresponds to the smallest admissible triple of consecutive
gaps.

*The key insight is* that genuine one-dimensional holes require at least three
points arranged non-collinearly, which on the gap side means a constraint on
consecutive gap *pairs* rather than single gaps.

*Why now?* The one-dimensional theory is now fully understood, so the natural
next obstruction — the first appearance of `H_1` — isolates exactly the
combinatorics of consecutive-gap patterns, a well-studied but topologically
unexploited object.

## 4. Barcode rigidity distinguishes primes from random gap models

**Conjecture.** The prime barcode differs measurably from that of a Poisson point
process of matching local intensity: the fraction of length-`2` bars stays
bounded away from the Poisson prediction, detectable purely from the barcode.

*The key insight is* that twin primes are anomalously frequent compared with a
memoryless gap model, and this anomaly survives as a persistent statistical
signature in the length-`2` bar count.

*Why now?* The exact identification of length-`2` bars with twin pairs gives a
clean, model-free statistic on which prime and Poisson barcodes can be compared
head to head.
directions.title: That the zero-dimensional persistent barcode of the prime

# Future Directions — Number Theory on Networks

This cycle established the spectral–arithmetic dictionary for the Ihara zeta function of a
`(q+1)`-regular graph: the local factor `1 − λu + qu²` obeys a functional equation under
`u ↦ 1/(qu)`, its zeros lie on the circle `|u| = 1/√q` exactly when the Ramanujan bound
`λ² ≤ 4q` holds, and for the cycle graph the whole determinant collapses to `(1 − uⁿ)²` via the
cyclotomic factorization. The following conjectures push the dictionary further.

## 1. The Ramanujan threshold is the unique real-zero boundary

**Conjecture.** For a `(q+1)`-regular graph, the number of adjacency eigenvalues violating the
Ramanujan bound `|λ| ≤ 2√q` equals the number of real zeros of the Ihara zeta on the interval
`(1/√q, 1)`, counted with multiplicity, and each such eigenvalue contributes exactly one
zero inside and one outside the critical circle.

*The key insight is* that the product of the two reciprocal zeros of every local factor is the
constant `1/q`, so a zero can leave the critical circle only in an inside/outside pair, making the
count of off-circle zeros a rigid invariant of the spectral gap.

*Why now?* The reciprocal-product law `α·β = q` and the real-root dichotomy across `λ² = 4q` are
now proved in full; the remaining step is a bookkeeping argument over the spectrum, well within
reach of the same real-analytic techniques.

## 2. A trace-formula bridge between prime cycles and eigenvalues

**Conjecture.** For a connected `(q+1)`-regular graph the logarithmic derivative of the Ihara zeta
expands as `u·d/du log ζ_G(u) = Σ_{m≥1} N_m uᵐ`, where `N_m` is the number of closed geodesics
of length `m`, and `N_m = Σ_j λ_jᵐ⁽ᵍᵉᵒ⁾` for the "geodesic eigenvalues" `λ_j⁽ᵍᵉᵒ⁾` obtained from
the reciprocal zeros of the determinant.

*The key insight is* that taking the logarithmic derivative of the determinant form turns the
product over the spectrum into a sum over the reciprocal zeros, converting a multiplicative
identity into an additive Selberg-type trace formula.

*Why now?* The determinant factorization into local factors and its functional equation are
established, giving the exact object whose logarithmic derivative produces the geodesic counts.

## 3. Cyclotomic collapse characterizes vertex-transitive circulants

**Conjecture.** Among connected `2`-regular-or-more circulant graphs, the Ihara zeta inverse
factors as a product of cyclotomic-type binomials `∏ (1 − uᵈ)^{eᵈ}` if and only if the graph is a
disjoint-free circulant whose connection set is closed under negation; the cycle `Cₙ` with its
clean `(1 − uⁿ)²` is the extremal minimal case.

*The key insight is* that the adjacency eigenvalues of a circulant are values of a fixed
trigonometric polynomial at the `n`-th roots of unity, so the determinant is a resultant that
factors through cyclotomy exactly when the connection set is symmetric.

*Why now?* The cycle case is proved via the roots-of-unity product, and the identical machinery
(difference of powers over `n`-th roots, inverse reindexing) applies verbatim to any symmetric
circulant connection set.

## 4. Ramanujan graphs saturate a determinant extremum

**Conjecture.** Over all `(q+1)`-regular graphs on `n` vertices, the quantity
`max_j |zero of local factor j| · min_j |zero|` is minimized precisely by the Ramanujan graphs,
where it equals `1/q` (all zeros on the circle), and every non-Ramanujan graph strictly exceeds it.

*The key insight is* that the critical circle is the simultaneous minimizer of the outer radius and
maximizer of the inner radius, so being Ramanujan is an extremal (isoperimetric-type) property of
the zeta zeros rather than merely a spectral-gap inequality.

*Why now?* We have proved both the on-circle law under the Ramanujan bound and the straddling
behavior when it fails; formulating the extremal statement is the natural synthesis of the two.
directions.title: Spectral–arithmetic dictionary for the Ihara zeta fun

# Future Directions

This project formalises the *algebraic skeleton* of the "topology of Bach"
mission: pitch-class space as `ℤ/12ℤ`, harmonic cycles as cyclic subgroups, and
the circle of fifths as the unique-up-to-symmetry longest such cycle. What is
proved is a self-contained, machine-checked chain:

1. `cycleLen_eq` — harmonic cycle length `= 12 / gcd(12, k)`.
2. Concrete values (fifth `12`, tritone `2`, third `3`, whole tone `6`, …).
3. `cycleLen_le`, `fifth_cycleLen_maximal`, `cycleLen_dvd_12` — the fifth is a
   longest cycle; every cycle length divides `12`.
4. `cycleLen_eq_12_iff`, `maximal_generators` — spanning intervals are exactly
   those coprime to `12`, namely `{1, 5, 7, 11}`.
5. `fifth_generates`, `generates_iff` — the fifth generates the whole
   pitch-class group; generation ⇔ coprimality.
6. `cof_hamiltonian` — the explicit circle of fifths is a Hamiltonian cycle.
7. `barLen`, `fifth_barLen_gt_half`, `tritone_barLen_lt_half` — the mission's
   normalised persistence-bar thresholds (Bach `> 0.5`, atonal `< 0.5`).

## Natural next steps

- **Genuine persistent homology.** Replace the proxy `cycleLen` with an actual
  Vietoris–Rips filtration on a finite metric pitch-class space (the "torus"
  metric `d(a,b) = min(|a-b|, 12-|a-b|)` on `ℤ/12ℤ`, or a weighted graph metric
  along fifths). Prove that `H₁` of the Rips complex is non-trivial at the scale
  where the circle-of-fifths cycle appears, and compute its birth/death. Mathlib
  now has simplicial/`SimplicialComplex` machinery to build on.

- **Betti numbers of circulant graphs.** The interval-`k` harmonic motion is a
  circulant graph `Cay(ℤ/12ℤ, {±k})`; its cycle structure and first Betti number
  `b₁ = |E| - |V| + (# components)` can be computed group-theoretically. Formalise
  `b₁` for these graphs and connect it to `cycleLen`.

- **Other temperaments.** Everything generalises from `12` to arbitrary `n`-tone
  equal temperament (`ℤ/nℤ`): the longest harmonic cycle has length `n`, attained
  exactly by intervals coprime to `n` (there are `φ(n)` of them). A parametrised
  version of `IntervalCycles.lean` over `ℤ/nℤ` would state and prove this in full
  generality (19-TET, 31-TET, etc.).

- **Voice-leading geometry.** Encode chords (not just single intervals) as
  multisets of pitch classes and study the orbifold `Tⁿ/Sₙ` of Tymoczko's
  voice-leading spaces; the circle of fifths reappears as a geodesic loop.

- **Empirical bridge.** Connect the normalised `barLen` thresholds to a real
  persistence computation over corpora (Bach chorales vs. pop vs. atonal),
  closing the loop with the mission's stated experiment.

# Future Directions

This project formalizes a **cross-domain bridge**: Sudoku (a constraint satisfaction problem)
is identified with proper vertex coloring (graph theory), and the shared structural invariant
— the number of symbols `n²` — is pinned down as the chromatic number of the Sudoku constraint
graph.

Main results in `Bridges/SudokuChromatic.lean`:

- `isSudokuSolution_iff_properColoring` — a filling is a valid Sudoku solution iff it is a
  proper coloring of the Sudoku constraint graph (the CSP ↔ graph-coloring bridge).
- `exists_isSudokuSolution` — every empty `n²×n²` Sudoku is solvable (`n ≥ 1`), by an explicit
  arithmetic construction.
- `sudokuGraph_colorable` — the constraint graph is `n²`-colorable.
- `firstRow_isClique` / `firstRow_card` — a full row is a clique of size `n²`.
- `sudokuGraph_chromaticNumber` — the chromatic number is exactly `n²`.

## Natural next steps

1. **Clique number and other invariants.** We proved `ω ≥ n²` via a full row and `χ = n²`.
   One could show `ω = n²` exactly (no larger clique exists), and compute the independence
   number and fractional chromatic number of the Sudoku graph.

2. **Counting solutions ↔ counting colorings.** The number of completed Sudoku grids equals
   the number of proper `n²`-colorings, i.e. the evaluation of the chromatic polynomial of the
   Sudoku graph at `n²`. Formalizing this connection would tie the enumeration of Sudoku grids
   (known for `9×9`: 6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960) to graph polynomials.

3. **Latin squares and partial bridges.** Dropping the block constraints yields the rook's
   graph, whose proper colorings are exactly Latin squares. The block constraints refine this;
   formalizing the tower rook-graph → Sudoku-graph would connect design theory to coloring.

4. **List coloring / precoloring extension.** A Sudoku *puzzle* (with clues) is a
   precoloring-extension problem. The NP-completeness of generalized Sudoku is exactly the
   NP-completeness of precoloring extension for this graph family — a bridge to complexity
   theory. Formalizing the reduction would make the "P vs NP of Sudoku" framing rigorous.

5. **The phase-transition conjecture.** The empirical claim that random instances undergo a
   solvability phase transition at clue density `d_c = (n²-1)/n²` is asymptotic and probabilistic;
   it is not a theorem and, to our knowledge, has no closed-form proof. A rigorous treatment
   would require second-moment / interpolation methods from the theory of random CSPs
   (analogous to random `k`-SAT thresholds). The chromatic-number invariant proved here is the
   deterministic backbone such an analysis would build on: the clique of `n²` mutually
   constrained cells is the local structure whose density governs hardness.

directions.description: The Robertson-Seymour theorem states that the set of finite graphs is well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation: any infinite sequence of graphs contains two where one is a minor of the other. This implies that any minor-closed graph property is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors. Conjecture: the same theorem holds for representable matroids over any finite field. Specifically, for any finite field F_q, the set of F_q-representable matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation. This would generalize the Robertson-Seymour theorem from graphs (F_2-representable matroids) to all finite fields. The conjecture is known to fail for general matroids (by the existence of infinite antichains of non-representable matroids), but for F_q-representable matroids with q <= 3, it is open. Conjecture: for F_3 (ternary matroids), the set of excluded minors for representability is finite. The current known excluded minors for F_3 are: the Fano matroid F_7, its dual F_7*, and the non-Pappus matroid. Test: enumerate ternary matroids of rank 3 on 9 elements, verify that all but the known excluded minors are F_3-representable. Impact: Robertson-Seymour for matroids would unify graph minor theory and matroid theory under a single well-quasi-ordering theorem.
directions.proof_strategy: Define matroid minor: M' is a minor of M if M' can be obtained from M by a sequence of deletions and contractions. The Robertson-Seymour theorem for graphs: for any infinite sequence G_1, G_2, ..., there exist i < j such that G_i is a minor of G_j. Conjecture: the same holds for F_q-representable matroids. For q=2 (graphs): this is Robertson-Seymour. For q=3: this is open. Known result: the set of excluded minors for F_3-representability is {F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus}. The conjecture would follow from: (1) F_3-representable matroids are well-quasi-ordered under the minor relation, and (2) any minor-closed class of F_3-representable matroids has finitely many excluded minors. Step (1) requires showing that F_3-representable matroids contain no infinite antichain. The known antichains (uniform matroids U_{2,n} for n >= 4) are NOT F_3-representable for large n. Step (2) follows from (1) by the same argument as Robertson-Seymour. Test: enumerate all rank-3 matroids on 9 elements (there are ~100), check F_3-representability, verify that excluded minors are exactly F_7, F_7*, non-Pappus.
directions.title: Matroid Minors and the Graph Theorem: Robertson-Seymour for Matroids

# Stochastic Galois Theory over Finite Fields — Results and Future Directions

## What was proved (all `sorry`-free, axioms `propext`/`Classical.choice`/`Quot.sound`)

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisRoots.lean` — the expected-roots identity.**
For a monic degree-`n` polynomial over a finite commutative ring `K` (`q = |K|`, `n ≥ 1`),
encoded by its coefficient vector `v : Fin n → K`,
```
∑ v, #{ r : K | monicEval n v r = 0 } = q^n            (total_root_incidences)
```
i.e. **the expected number of roots of a uniformly random monic degree-`n` polynomial is
exactly `1`**. The proof is a clean double count: swap the sum over polynomials with the
sum over base points, and observe that for a fixed `r` exactly `q^{n-1}` polynomials
vanish at `r` (the constant coefficient is forced). A specialization
`total_root_incidences_zmod` phrases it over `F_p`.

This is the cleanest universally-true instance of the "random polynomial = random
permutation" dictionary: roots ↔ linear factors ↔ **fixed points of the Frobenius
permutation**, and a uniform permutation in `S_n` also has exactly one fixed point on
average.

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisDegreeTwo.lean` — exact degree-2 statistics.**
Over a finite field `K` of odd characteristic (`q = |K|`):
```
2 · #{ reducible quadratics }   = q(q+1)                (card_reducible)
2 · #{ irreducible quadratics } = q(q-1)                (card_irreducible)
#{ quadratics with a repeated root } = q                (card_double_root)
```
proved from the two structural facts `sum_nroots` (total incidences `= q^2`) and
`nroots_le_two` (a quadratic has `≤ 2` roots), via completing the square
(`nroots_eq_disc`) and the square-root count lemmas. Consequences: proportion irreducible
`→ 1/2` (the `S_2` `2`-cycle fraction) and proportion with vanishing discriminant `= 1/q`.

**`Catalog/Novelty/StochasticGaloisCyclic.lean` — a structural correction.**
```
IsEmpty ((L ≃ₐ[K] L) ≃* Equiv.Perm (Fin n))   for finite L and n ≥ 3   (finiteField_gal_ne_symm)
```
Over a finite field every Galois group is cyclic (Frobenius), hence abelian, hence never
isomorphic to the non-abelian `S_n` for `n ≥ 3`. The prompt's conjecture that
`P(Gal = S_n) → 1` is therefore false at the group-theoretic level: `P(Gal = S_n) = 0`
for `n ≥ 3`. What survives is the *cycle-type/factorization* heuristic, not the
"maximal group" one.

## The corrected picture

Over `ℚ`, Hilbert irreducibility gives `Gal = S_n` for almost all polynomials. Over `F_q`
this fails: Galois groups are cyclic. The right analogue is **Frobenius equidistribution**
— the factorization type of a random monic degree-`n` polynomial (the cycle type of
Frobenius on the roots) is distributed like the cycle type of a uniform random permutation
in `S_n` as `q → ∞`. The proved theorems are the two cleanest exact cases of this:
the fixed-point count in all degrees, and the complete `n = 2` distribution.

## Concrete next steps

1. **Degree-3 full distribution.** Prove `#{irreducible monic cubics} = (q^3 - q)/3` and
   the split of reducible cubics into `(x-r)(x-s)(x-t)` types, matching the `S_3` cycle
   distribution `{3-cycles : 1/3, transpositions : 1/2, identity : 1/6}` in the limit. The
   incidence method here generalizes: also count `∑ (#roots choose 2)` to access pair
   statistics.

2. **Gauss's formula in general.** Formalize `I_q(n) = (1/n) ∑_{d|n} μ(d) q^{n/d}` for the
   number of monic irreducibles of degree `n` over `F_q`, giving proportion `→ 1/n`, the
   `n`-cycle fraction. Mathlib has `X^{q^n} - X` factoring through irreducibles of degree
   `d | n`; the Möbius inversion is the missing piece.

3. **Higher moments / cycle index.** Prove that the `k`-th factorial moment of the number
   of degree-`1` factors tends to `1` (Poisson(1) limit), the polynomial shadow of the
   fixed-point Poisson law for random permutations. The `k = 1` case is exactly
   `total_root_incidences`; `k = 2` needs the ordered-pair incidence count.

4. **Squarefree density.** Prove `#{monic squarefree degree-n} = q^n - q^{n-1}` for
   `n ≥ 2` (discriminant `≠ 0`), so the non-separable proportion is exactly `1/q` — the
   general-`n` version of `card_double_root`, and the honest reading of the prompt's
   `P(discriminant = 0)` claim.

5. **Chebotarev over `F_q(t)`.** Frame the above as the function-field Chebotarev density
   theorem for `S_n`-covers, connecting to the arithmetic (rather than geometric)
   monodromy that genuinely can be `S_n`.

# Future Directions — Morphogenesis as Algebraic Geometry

The linear analysis established here recasts the onset of Turing patterns as
conic-section geometry: the number of excited spatial modes is an algebraic degree,
and the boundedness of the background level set separates spots from stripes and
labyrinths. Several bold, testable conjectures follow.

## 1. The genus dictionary

**Conjecture.** For a pattern generated by `k` spatial modes, the background level
set is (generically) a smooth real curve whose complexification has genus at most
`(k−1)(k−2)/2`, and the number of bounded ovals equals the number of distinct spot
families in the pattern.

*The key insight is* that the mode count fixes the degree of the defining polynomial,
and the classical genus–degree formula then caps the topological complexity, turning a
statement about pattern topology into an inequality about polynomial degree.

*Why now?* The degree correspondence for single modes (Chebyshev) is fully in hand,
so the remaining step is purely the theory of real plane curves — a mature subject —
applied to explicitly known low-degree families.

## 2. Sharp mode–degree equality

**Conjecture.** A superposition of `k` modes with a nonzero top harmonic has a level
set of algebraic degree *exactly* `k` in the Chebyshev coordinates, and no
reparametrisation lowers this degree.

*The key insight is* that the leading coefficient of the `k`-th Chebyshev polynomial
is `2^{k-1} ≠ 0`, so the top mode cannot be cancelled by lower ones — degree is a
faithful invariant of mode count.

*Why now?* The exact-degree statement is already proved for a single mode and for the
squared three-mode amplitude; extending it to arbitrary superpositions needs only
leading-term bookkeeping, which is tractable.

## 3. Hexagons are sextics

**Conjecture.** Every hexagonally symmetric two-dimensional Turing pattern has a
background level set defined by a sextic curve invariant under the order-6 dihedral
group, and conversely every such invariant sextic is realised by a three-mode
reaction–diffusion system.

*The key insight is* that three modes reach degree six, and the hexagonal symmetry
group acts on degree-six invariants with exactly the dimension needed to parametrise
the observed patterns.

*Why now?* The degree-six ceiling for three-mode systems is established; the missing
ingredient is an invariant-theory computation of dihedral-invariant sextics, which is
finite-dimensional and explicit.

## 4. Boundedness is a bifurcation invariant

**Conjecture.** Along a reaction–diffusion bifurcation path, the transition from spot
to labyrinth morphology coincides exactly with the moment the defining quadratic form
loses definiteness (its discriminant changes sign), and this transition is detectable
from the reaction kinetics alone.

*The key insight is* that boundedness of a conic level set is controlled by the sign
of the quadratic form's discriminant, so a morphological phase transition is an
algebraic sign change rather than a delicate PDE phenomenon.

*Why now?* We have proved the two endpoints of this transition — definite forms give
bounded spots, indefinite forms give unbounded labyrinths — so the conjecture is the
natural interpolation and is amenable to explicit discriminant tracking.

## 5. Three-dimensional morphogenesis as algebraic surfaces

**Conjecture.** In three spatial dimensions, a `k`-mode Turing pattern has a
background level set that is a real algebraic surface of degree `k`, and the Turing
"gyroid" and "diamond" phases correspond to specific cubic and quartic surfaces.

*The key insight is* that the Chebyshev correspondence is dimension-agnostic: each
axial mode contributes one polynomial degree, so multi-dimensional patterns inherit
the same degree = mode-count law, now for surfaces.

*Why now?* The one-dimensional degree law and the planar conic dichotomy are proved;
lifting to surfaces reuses the same Chebyshev machinery with additional coordinates.

# Future Directions: Topological Quantum Compiling via Braid Groups

## What this project establishes (all machine-checked, no `sorry`, no extra axioms)

Working with the **reduced Burau representation** of the braid group `B₄` — which
is genuinely `3 × 3` — over an arbitrary commutative ring with parameter `t`,
`BurauB4.lean` proves:

1. **It is a representation of `B₄`.** All Artin braid relations hold for every
   `t`: `σ₁σ₂σ₁ = σ₂σ₁σ₂`, `σ₂σ₃σ₂ = σ₃σ₂σ₃`, `σ₁σ₃ = σ₃σ₁`, and each generator
   has determinant `−t` (invertible when `t` is a unit).
2. **The image is infinite.** At `t = −1` the element `ρ(σ₁σ₃)` is a nontrivial
   unipotent `I + N` (`N ≠ 0`, `N² = 0`), so `ρ(σ₁σ₃)ⁿ = I + nN`, its powers are
   pairwise distinct, and it has infinite order in `SL₃(ℤ)`.
3. **The image is non-abelian.** `ρ(σ₁)ρ(σ₂) ≠ ρ(σ₂)ρ(σ₁)`, hence the image
   cannot lie inside any abelian (maximal-torus) closed subgroup.
4. **Contrarian result — universality is parameter-dependent.** At `t = 1` every
   generator is an involution and the representation collapses to the finite
   permutation action of `S₄`. So "braiding is universal" is *false* for a generic
   parameter; the conjecture can hold only at special roots of unity. This is a
   concrete refutation of the naive universal reading.

## Honest gap versus the stated conjecture

The prompt's conjecture ("`ρ₅(B₄)` is dense in `SU(3)`") has two features that we
did **not** (and with current formalized mathematics essentially *cannot*)
establish directly:

* **Topological density in a Lie group.** Proving a finitely generated subgroup
  is dense in `SU(3)` requires the classification of closed subgroups of a
  compact connected Lie group plus a Zariski-density / Lie-algebra-generation
  argument, together with Solovay–Kitaev for the effective statement. Mathlib
  does not yet have this machinery packaged for `SU(3)`.
* **The unitary specialization.** The reduced Burau matrices are unitary only
  after conjugating by the (parameter-dependent) Hermitian Burau form and
  normalizing the determinant; the `t = −1` specialization we use for
  infiniteness lands in `SL₃(ℤ)`, not literally in `SU(3)`. Establishing
  unitarity at `t = e^{2πi/5}` is a separate finite computation over `ℂ`.

Also note a factual inconsistency in the prompt itself: the dimension formula
`U((k−1)(n−1)+1)` gives `U(13)` for `k=5, n=4`, not `U(3)`. The correct
`3`-dimensional object is the *reduced Burau* representation used here (Fibonacci
anyons on 4 strands do have a small fusion space, and the reduced Burau
dimension `n−1 = 3` is the honest match).

## Concrete next steps

1. **Unitarity at the physical root of unity.** Define the Hermitian Burau form
   `J(t)` and prove `ρ(σᵢ)* J ρ(σᵢ) = J` at `t = e^{2πi/5}`; deduce the image
   lands in `U(3)` (and in `SU(3)` after scaling by `(−t)^{−1/…}`).
2. **Infinite order at the root of unity.** Show a specific braid word has an
   eigenvalue that is an irrational rotation (argument an irrational multiple of
   `π`), giving infinite order directly inside `SU(3)` rather than via `SL₃(ℤ)`.
3. **Zariski density.** Prove the Lie algebra generated by `log ρ(σᵢ)` is all of
   `su(3)`; this is the algebraic heart of density and is finite linear algebra
   over `ℝ`, plausibly formalizable.
4. **From Zariski-dense to topologically dense.** Import/develop the theorem that
   a Zariski-dense subgroup of a compact simple Lie group is topologically dense
   — the remaining Lie-theoretic input.
5. **General `Bₙ`.** The definitions here extend verbatim to the `(n−1)`-
   dimensional reduced Burau representation of `Bₙ`; the braid-relation proofs
   should generalize with an indexed family of block matrices.

directions.description: The Collatz map T: N -> N defined by T(n) = n/2 if n even, 3n+1 if n odd, is conjectured to always reach 1. The Collatz conjecture is equivalent to: the orbit of every n under T eventually reaches the cycle {1, 4, 2, 1}. Define the Collatz Fourier transform: F_T(omega) = sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n} for N large. Conjecture: F_T has a spectral gap: |F_T(omega)| < C for all irrational omega, where C < sqrt(N). This would mean that the Collatz map does not concentrate energy at any irrational frequency — it is 'mixing' in the Fourier sense. Moreover, the spectral gap is related to the convergence rate: the wider the gap, the faster the orbit reaches 1. Conjecture: for the orbit of n, the number of steps to reach 1 is O(log(n)), which is equivalent to F_T having a spectral gap of width Omega(1/log(n)). Test: compute F_T for n up to 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with the spectral gaps of related maps (5n+1, 7n+1) which do NOT always converge. Impact: the Collatz conjecture is a spectral gap problem. Convergence to 1 means the Fourier transform has no resonances at irrational frequencies.
directions.proof_strategy: Define F_T(omega) = (1/N) * sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{2*pi*i*omega*T(n)/n}. For rational omega = p/q: F_T(p/q) measures the correlation between T(n)/n and the frequency p/q. For T(n) = n/2 (even case) or T(n) = (3n+1)/2 (odd case, accelerating), the ratio T(n)/n is either 1/2 or approximately 3/2 + 1/(2n). The spectral gap of F_T is: gap = inf_{|omega|>0} |F_T(omega)| / F_T(0). For a mixing map, F_T(omega) -> 0 as N -> infinity for irrational omega. This is the von Neumann ergodic theorem for the 3n+1 map. If the 3n+1 map is mixing (which is conjectured but not known), then F_T has a spectral gap. The connection to Collatz convergence: if T is mixing, then the orbit of n visits the set {1} with positive density, which implies it eventually reaches 1. The spectral gap width determines the convergence rate: a gap of width delta gives convergence in O(log(n)/delta) steps. Test: compute F_T(omega) for N = 10^6 and measure the spectral gap. Compare with 5n+1 (which has orbits that may diverge) and n+1 (which converges in n steps).
directions.title: The Fourier Analysis of Collatz: Spectral Gaps in the 3n+1 Map

# Future Directions: Chaos and Cryptography via the Logistic Map

This cycle established the exact semiconjugacy `f(sin² t) = sin²(2 t)` of the
full-strength logistic map `f(x) = 4x(1-x)` to angle doubling, and derived from
it (i) sensitive dependence on initial conditions with an explicit collapsing
family of seeds, and (ii) the exponential algebraic degree `2ⁿ` of the `n`-th
iterate. The following conjectures push the "chaos is cryptography" program
forward.

## 1. The conjugate coordinate breaks the naive chaos cipher in linear time

**Conjecture.** Recovering the seed of a logistic keystream is *not* as hard as
solving a degree-`2ⁿ` polynomial: in the conjugate coordinate `t` where
`x = sin²(π t)`, the map is the binary shift `t ↦ 2t (mod 1)`, so each iterate
merely reveals one more bit of `t`. Consequently the seed is recoverable to `n`
bits of precision from `O(n)` keystream samples with `O(n)` arithmetic, i.e. in
time polynomial in the security parameter.

*The key insight is* that the very degree-`2ⁿ` structure advertised as a hardness
barrier is an artifact of the wrong coordinate system; conjugacy linearizes the
apparent nonlinearity and collapses the exponential to a shift.

*Why now?* We have proved the exact conjugacy that makes the coordinate change
rigorous rather than heuristic, so the cryptanalytic reduction can be stated and
verified as a theorem rather than asserted.

## 2. The invariant density is the arcsine law, and it is the unique absolutely
continuous invariant measure

**Conjecture.** The measure `dμ = dx / (π √(x(1-x)))` on `(0,1)` is invariant
under `f`, is the pushforward of the uniform (Lebesgue/Haar) measure on the
doubling circle under `t ↦ sin²(π t)`, and is the unique `f`-invariant measure
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

*The key insight is* that ergodic-theoretic "randomness" of the keystream is
exactly the equidistribution of the doubling map transported through the
conjugacy; the biased arcsine density — not a uniform one — is what a raw
logistic keystream actually emits, revealing an exploitable statistical bias.

*Why now?* The conjugacy to angle doubling is in hand, so the invariance and
uniqueness reduce to known equidistribution facts for the doubling map pulled
back along a smooth change of variables.

## 3. Sensitivity gives a matching decryption-instability lower bound

**Conjecture.** For every seed there exist perturbations of size `ε` whose
`n`-th iterates differ by a constant `c > 0` once `n ≥ log₂(1/ε) + O(1)`, and
this threshold is tight: below it the outputs differ by `O(2ⁿ ε)`. Hence any
finite-precision implementation with `p` bits loses all correlation with the true
orbit after exactly `p` steps — the period and the sensitivity horizon coincide.

*The key insight is* that the stretching factor `2ⁿ` controls both the divergence
rate (from above) and the precision-loss rate (from below), so avalanche speed
and numerical unreliability are two readings of the same Lyapunov exponent
`log 2`.

*Why now?* We have an explicit seed family realizing the `O(1)` separation after
linearly many steps; upgrading it to a two-sided bound needs only the mean-value
control of `f'` that the conjugacy supplies.

## 4. Polynomial iterates factor through Chebyshev-type structure

**Conjecture.** The degree-`2ⁿ` iterate polynomials `fⁿ` are affinely conjugate
to the Chebyshev polynomials `T_{2ⁿ}`, and their real roots (the pre-images of a
fixed point) are exactly `sin²(kπ/2ⁿ⁺¹)` for the appropriate range of `k`,
equidistributed with the arcsine law of Conjecture 2.

*The key insight is* that both the logistic map and the Chebyshev family are
semiconjugate to angle doubling, so they must coincide up to an affine change of
variable, turning "solve a degree-`2ⁿ` equation" into "read off `2ⁿ` explicit
trigonometric roots."

*Why now?* The polynomial-iterate degree theorem and the trigonometric
conjugacy are both established here, so the identification of roots is a direct
consequence rather than a numerical observation.

forward.

## 1. The conjugate coordinate breaks the naive chaos cipher in linear time

**Conjecture.** Recovering the seed of a logistic keystream is *not* as hard as
solving a degree-`2ⁿ` polynomial: in the conjugate coordinate `t` where
`x = sin²(π t)`, the map is the binary shift `t ↦ 2t (mod 1)`, so each iterate
merely reveals one more bit of `t`. Consequently the seed is recoverable to `n`
bits of precision from `O(n)` keystream samples with `O(n)` arithmetic, i.e. in
time polynomial in the security parameter.

*The key insight is* that the very degree-`2ⁿ` structure advertised as a hardness
barrier is an artifact of the wrong coordinate system; conjugacy linearizes the
apparent nonlinearity and collapses the exponential to a shift.

*Why now?* We have proved the exact conjugacy that makes the coordinate change
rigorous rather than heuristic, so the cryptanalytic reduction can be stated and
verified as a theorem rather than asserted.

## 2. The invariant density is the arcsine law, and it is the unique absolutely
continuous invariant measure

**Conjecture.** The measure `dμ = dx / (π √(x(1-x)))` on `(0,1)` is invariant
under `f`, is the pushforward of the uniform (Lebesgue/Haar) measure on the
doubling circle under `t ↦ sin²(π t)`, and is the unique `f`-invariant measure
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

*The key insight is* that ergodic-theoretic "randomness" of the keystream is
exactly the equidistribution of the doubling map transported through the
conjugacy; the biased arcsine density — not a uniform one — is what a raw
logistic keystream actually emits, revealing an exploitable statistical bias.

*Why now?* The conjugacy to angle doubling is in hand, so the invariance and
uniqueness reduce to known equidistribution facts for the doubling map pulled
back along a smooth change of variables.

## 3. Sensitivity gives a matching decryption-instability lower bound

**Conjecture.** For every seed there exist perturbations of size `ε` whose
`n`-th iterates differ by a constant `c > 0` once `n ≥ log₂(1/ε) + O(1)`, and
this threshold is tight: below it the outputs differ by `O(2ⁿ ε)`. Hence any
finite-precision implementation with `p` bits loses all correlation with the true
orbit after exactly `p` steps — the period and the sensitivity horizon coincide.

*The key insight is* that the stretching factor `2ⁿ` controls both the divergence
rate (from above) and the precision-loss rate (from below), so avalanche speed
and numerical unreliability are two readings of the same Lyapunov exponent
`log 2`.

*Why now?* We have an explicit seed family realizing the `O(1)` separation after
linearly many steps; upgrading it to a two-sided bound needs only the mean-value
control of `f'` that the conjugacy supplies.

## 4. Polynomial iterates factor through Chebyshev-type structure

**Conjecture.** The degree-`2ⁿ` iterate polynomials `fⁿ` are affinely conjugate
to the Chebyshev polynomials `T_{2ⁿ}`, and their real roots (the pre-images of a
fixed point) are exactly `sin²(kπ/2ⁿ⁺¹)` for the appropriate range of `k`,
equidistributed with the arcsine law of Conjecture 2.

*The key insight is* that both the logistic map and the Chebyshev family are
semiconjugate to angle doubling, so they must coincide up to an affine change of
variable, turning "solve a degree-`2ⁿ` equation" into "read off `2ⁿ` explicit
trigonometric roots."

*Why now?* The polynomial-iterate degree theorem and the trigonometric
conjugacy are both established here, so the identification of roots is a direct
consequence rather than a numerical observation.

# Future Directions: Homological Quantum Codes

This cycle established the exact dictionary "logical qubits = middle homology"
for the chain-complex model of CSS codes, and used it to compute the logical
dimension of the hypercube homological code, refuting the folklore "one qubit"
law for the hypercube *graph*. The following conjectures extend those findings.

## 1. The distance of the hypercube homological code

**Conjecture.** For the hypercube graph `Qₙ` (`n ≥ 2`), the homological code
`HQECC(Qₙ)` has minimum distance equal to the girth of `Qₙ`, namely `4`,
independent of `n`; consequently it does **not** achieve the quantum Singleton
bound `d = 2^{n/2}` for `n ≥ 5`.

The key insight is that in a one-dimensional complex the shortest nontrivial
cycle is a shortest graph cycle, and every hypercube contains a 4-cycle while
containing no triangle. Distance is therefore a girth invariant, decoupled from
the exponentially large number of encoded qubits computed in this cycle.

Why now? The present cycle pins down the encoded dimension `β₁(Qₙ) = 2ⁿ⁻¹(n−2)+1`
exactly; the natural next parameter is the distance, and the girth heuristic is
directly testable on the same family that already contradicted the qubit count.

## 2. Euler characteristic as a code-rate obstruction

**Conjecture.** For any connected graph complex, the code rate `k/n` of its
homological code equals `1 − (V−1)/E`, and among all connected graphs on a fixed
number of edges the rate is maximized precisely by graphs with a single vertex
of many loops (bouquets) and minimized by trees (rate `0`).

The key insight is that the Euler identity `β₀ − β₁ = V − E`, proved this cycle,
turns the rate into a purely combinatorial ratio; extremizing it is a discrete
isoperimetric problem on the vertex/edge counts.

Why now? The Euler identity was just established in full additive generality over
an arbitrary field, so the rate formula is an immediate corollary awaiting an
extremal analysis.

## 3. Every finite-dimensional homology group is a logical space

**Conjecture.** For every field `K` and every pair of natural numbers `k ≤ n`
there is a length-two chain complex over `K` with middle space of dimension `n`
whose homology has dimension exactly `k`; hence every logical/physical dimension
pair `(k, n)` is realized by some CSS chain complex.

The key insight is that the dimension formula `k = n − rank d₁ − rank d₂` proved
this cycle is not just an inequality but an exact accounting, so realizability
reduces to choosing two maps with prescribed ranks summing to `n − k`.

Why now? With the exact dimension theorem in hand, the realizability question
becomes a rank-prescription problem in linear algebra rather than a homological
mystery.

## 4. Cohomological duality of the two check families

**Conjecture.** For a CSS chain complex the `X`-logical space `ker d₁ / im d₂`
and the `Z`-logical space `ker d₂ᵀ / im d₁ᵀ` have equal dimension, and this common
dimension is a self-dual topological invariant of the complex.

The key insight is that transposition exchanges kernels and cokernels while
preserving ranks, so the dimension formula forces the two homologies to match;
CSS self-duality is thus a shadow of rank symmetry.

Why now? The additive rank-nullity backbone developed this cycle applies verbatim
to the transposed complex, making the duality statement a direct next theorem
rather than a separate development.
directions.title: Exact dictionary "logical qubits = middle homology"

directions.description: Sperner's lemma states that any proper coloring of a triangulated simplex with n+1 colors has at least one fully colored simplex. This is a combinatorial analog of Brouwer's fixed point theorem. Nash's theorem states that every finite game has a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium, proved using Kakutani's fixed point theorem. Conjecture: Sperner's lemma directly implies Nash's theorem. Specifically, given an n-player game with strategies S_1, ..., S_n, construct the n-simplex Delta = Delta(S_1 x ... x S_n) of mixed strategy profiles. Define a Sperner coloring of Delta by: color vertex v with color i if player i's best response to v is strategy i. By Sperner's lemma, there exists a fully colored simplex. The center of this simplex is an approximate Nash equilibrium (each player is approximately best-responding). Taking the limit as the triangulation gets finer gives an exact Nash equilibrium. Conjecture: this construction gives a constructive proof of Nash's theorem that yields a triangulation-based algorithm for finding Nash equilibria with complexity O(N^{n}) where N is the total number of pure strategies. Test: implement the Sperner-based algorithm for 2-player games and verify it finds all Nash equilibria. Impact: Nash equilibria are combinatorial fixed points. Sperner's lemma is the fundamental theorem of game theory.
directions.proof_strategy: Given an n-player game G with strategy sets S_1, ..., S_n. Define the simplex Delta = {(p_1, ..., p_n) : p_i in Delta(S_i), sum p_i = 1}. Define Sperner coloring c: Delta -> {1, ..., n} by c(v) = i where i = argmax_j BR_i(v)_j (player i's best response to v has highest probability on strategy j). Boundary condition: if v is on the face where p_i = 0, then c(v) != i (a player with zero probability cannot have a best response there). Wait, the correct boundary condition is: if v is on the face where v_i = 0, then c(v) is not i. Sperner's lemma: there exists at least one fully colored simplex (with all colors 1, ..., n). The center of this simplex is an epsilon-Nash equilibrium where epsilon depends on the mesh size of the triangulation. As mesh -> 0, epsilon -> 0, giving an exact Nash equilibrium. Algorithm: triangulate Delta with mesh epsilon, color vertices by best responses, find fully colored simplex by Sperner's lemma (using the path-following algorithm). Complexity: O((1/epsilon)^{n-1} * |S|) per iteration. Test: implement for 2x2 games (Matching Pennies, Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes). Verify that the algorithm finds the unique Nash equilibrium.
directions.title: Sperner's Lemma Implies Nash Equilibria: Combinatorial Fixed Points in Game Theory

# Future Directions

This cycle deepened the "Graph Coloring with Emotions" thread from a qualitative invariant
(`emoChrom`, the emotional chromatic number) to a **quantitative closed form**: the full chromatic
polynomial of the friendship (windmill) graph.

## What was proved (`Catalog/Novelty/FriendshipChromaticPolynomial.lean`)

- `chromVal_friendship` : `P(F_n, q) = q · ((q-1)(q-2))^n` for all `n, q`, via an explicit bijection
  (`frEquiv`) between proper colourings and (centre colour) × (per-triangle admissible pair), whose
  fibre count `(q-1)(q-2)` is established in `pairColors_card`.
- `friendship_chromVal_six` : `P(F_n, 6) = 6 · 20^n` — the original conjecture (six basic emotions).
- `chromVal_pos_iff_colorable`, `friendship_colorable_three`, `friendship_colorable_six`,
  `friendship_not_colorable_two`, `friendship_chromaticNumber` (`χ(F_n) = 3` for `n ≥ 1`).

## Also proved (`Catalog/Novelty/FriendshipEmotionalChromaticNumber.lean`)

The bridge to the emotional-chromatic-number invariant (former next step 6, now **done**):

- `emoChrom_friendship` : `emoChrom (F_n) = 3` for every `n`, obtained by feeding
  `friendship_colorable_three` into `emoChrom_eq_three_iff`.
- `emoChrom_friendship_within_window` : `3 ≤ emoChrom (F_n) ≤ 6` — every friendship network sits
  inside the six-basic-emotions window.
- `chromVal_emoChrom_friendship` : `P(F_n, emoChrom (F_n)) = 3 · 2^n`.
- `emoChrom_eq_chromaticNumber_friendship` : for `n ≥ 1`, `emoChrom (F_n) = χ(F_n)` (both `3`).

## Natural next steps

1. **Generalized windmills `Wd(m, n)`** (`n` copies of `K_m` glued at a vertex): the same bijection
   generalizes to `P = q · (q-1)^{\underline{m-1}}{}^{\,n}` where `(q-1)^{\underline{m-1}}` is the
   falling factorial `(q-1)(q-2)···(q-m+1)`. The friendship graph is the `m = 3` case.
2. **Book graphs / fans / gear graphs**: other one-common-vertex gluings with clean product forms.
3. **Deletion–contraction cross-check**: rederive `chromVal_friendship` from the recurrence in
   `Catalog/Combinatorics/ChromaticPolynomial.lean` (deleting/contracting one triangle edge) and
   prove the two derivations agree, tightening the bridge between the counting and algebraic views.
4. **Polynomiality and roots**: lift `chromVal` to a genuine `Polynomial ℤ` and show its integer
   roots are exactly `{0, 1, 2}`, matching the emotional floor `emoChrom = 3`.
5. **Coefficient combinatorics**: expand `q·((q-1)(q-2))^n` and connect the alternating-sign
   coefficients to Whitney's broken-circuit theorem for this graph family.
6. **Bridge to `emoChrom`** — *done*, see `Catalog/Novelty/FriendshipEmotionalChromaticNumber.lean`
   (`emoChrom_friendship : emoChrom (F_n) = 3`, extended to the whole family, plus the
   window and chromatic-number consequences).

# Future directions

This project formalizes the *order-theoretic bridge* connecting structural
graph/matroid theory (Robertson–Seymour forbidden minors) with commutative
algebra (Dickson's lemma / finite generation of monomial ideals). The single
theorem `WQOFiniteBasis.exists_finite_generating_family` — every upper set of a
well-quasi-order is generated by its finite antichain of minimal elements —
specializes to both, and its dual `exists_finite_forbidden_family` is the
abstract Robertson–Seymour corollary.

Files:
- `Catalog/Novelty/ExcludedMinors/WellQuasiOrderFiniteBasis.lean` — the abstract
  WQO finite-basis engine (Robertson–Seymour / Dickson bridge).
- `Catalog/Novelty/ExcludedMinors/ZnGain.lean` — a concrete, fully proved
  excluded-minor instance: over every cyclic group `ℤ/n` (`n ≥ 2`) the
  parallel-class slice of the Zaslavsky/Funk conjecture holds with single
  excluded minor `(n+1)K₂` (`digon_excluded_minor`), together with the
  divisibility monotonicity law `gainable_mono_of_dvd`. This realizes, in one
  concrete family, the "explicit minor order + forbidden minor" pattern that the
  abstract engine describes in general.

## Natural next steps

1. **Instantiate to an explicit minor order on matroids.** Build a `PartialOrder`
   on (isomorphism classes of) matroids from the minor relation, so that
   `robertson_seymour_of_wqo` applies literally to a Lean `Matroid` type. The
   hard input — that a given class is WQO — would remain a hypothesis, but the
   forbidden-minor corollary would then be a genuine matroid statement.

2. **Formalize the graph-minor `PartialOrder`.** Similarly, equip finite
   `SimpleGraph`s (up to isomorphism) with the minor order and derive the finite
   forbidden-minor characterization of any minor-closed graph property, *given*
   the Robertson–Seymour WQO hypothesis.

3. **Dickson → Hilbert basis theorem.** Connect `dickson` to Mathlib's monomial
   ideals: show the minimal-generator set produced here is a generating set of
   the corresponding `MonomialIdeal`, recovering finite generation as a corollary
   and linking to Gröbner-basis infrastructure.

4. **Higman's lemma.** Extend from the finite product `Fin k → ℕ` to the WQO of
   finite words / `List` over a WQO alphabet (Higman's lemma). Mathlib already
   has some `PartiallyWellOrderedOn` machinery for subsequences; combining it
   with the finite-basis engine here would give finite obstruction sets for
   subword-closed languages.

5. **Kruskal's tree theorem** as a further WQO input, feeding the same
   finite-obstruction corollary for tree-minor-closed families.

6. **Effective / decidable versions.** For decidable minor tests and finite
   ambient data, turn the abstract finite `Set` of obstructions into a concrete
   `Finset`, yielding a decision procedure schema for membership in a
   minor-closed class.

## Scope note

The deep theorems (Robertson–Seymour itself; Geelen–Gerards–Whittle WQO for
`F_q`-representable matroids) are the *hypotheses* consumed by the bridge, not
its conclusions. The contribution here is the reusable engine that converts any
such WQO input into the finite forbidden-minor / finite-generation output, made
fully formal and axiom-clean in Lean 4 + Mathlib.

directions.description: A periodic rhythm in music is a function f: Z -> {0, 1} that is periodic: f(n + p) = f(n) for some period p. The symmetry group of a rhythm with period p is a subgroup of Z/pZ. But music also has 2D patterns: a drum pattern is a function g: Z x Z -> {0, 1} (onset grid in time x pitch). The symmetry group of a drum pattern is a subgroup of Z x Z, which is a wallpaper group in 1D. In 2D, the wallpaper groups classify all possible symmetries of periodic patterns. There are exactly 17 wallpaper groups in 2D. Conjecture: the 17 wallpaper groups correspond to 17 fundamentally different types of rhythmic structure in music. Specifically: (1) p1: no symmetry (free rhythm), (2) p2: 2-fold rotational symmetry (call-and-response), (3) pm: mirror symmetry (palindrome), (4) pg: glide reflection (canon), (5) cm: mirror + glide (round), (6) pmm: double mirror (bilateral palindrome), (7) pmg: mirror + glide (inverted canon), (8) pgg: double glide (double canon), (9) cmm: double mirror + glide (round + palindrome), (10) p4: 4-fold rotation (4-bar cycle), (11) p4m: 4-fold + mirrors (variations on a theme), (12) p4g: 4-fold + glides (inverted variations), (13) p3: 3-fold rotation (3-bar blues), (14) p3m1: 3-fold + mirrors, (15) p31m: 3-fold + glides, (16) p6: 6-fold rotation (whole-tone scale symmetry), (17) p6m: 6-fold + mirrors (maximal symmetry, the 'perfect' rhythm). Test: classify 1000 drum patterns by their wallpaper group and verify the distribution matches musical practice. Impact: there are exactly 17 types of rhythm in music, classified by the wallpaper groups.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a drum pattern as a function g: Z_m x Z_n -> {0, 1} (onset grid with m time steps and n pitch classes). The symmetry group of g is the set of (a, b, R) in Z_m x Z_n x D_n such that g(R*x + a, R*y + b) = g(x, y) for all (x, y). Here D_n is the dihedral group of order 2n. For 2D patterns with translation lattice L, the symmetry group is a wallpaper group. The 17 wallpaper groups are: p1, p2, pm, pg, cm, pmm, pmg, pgg, cmm, p4, p4m, p4g, p3, p3m1, p31m, p6, p6m. Each corresponds to a different type of rhythmic symmetry. p1: no symmetry (most common in free jazz). p2: 2-fold rotation (AABB form). pm: mirror (palindromic, like 'I Palindrome I' by They Might Be Giants). pg: glide (canon, like 'Row Row Row Your Boat'). p4: 4-fold (4/4 time with 4-bar phrases). p6: 6-fold (6/8 time with whole-tone symmetry). p6m: maximal symmetry (only achievable with hexagonal grids, corresponds to the most symmetric possible rhythm). Test: encode 1000 drum patterns as 2D grids, compute their symmetry groups, classify into the 17 wallpaper groups, and compare with musical genre.
directions.title: Crystallographic Groups and Music: The 17 Wallpaper Groups of Rhythm

directions.description: A cellular automaton (CA) rule f: A^Z -> A^Z is a function from configurations to configurations. The CA is reversible if f is bijective. By Hedlund's theorem, a CA is reversible iff its local rule is a permutation. But which CA rules have reversible dynamics? Conjecture: the set of reversible CA rules of radius r on alphabet A is a group under composition, isomorphic to a subgroup of S_{|A|^{2r+1}}. Specifically, the reversibility group G(r, A) is the subgroup of S_{|A|^{2r+1}} generated by the local rules of all reversible CAs of radius r. Conjecture: for binary CAs (A = {0, 1}) with radius r, G(r, {0, 1}) = S_{2^{2r+1}} for r >= 2. This means that any permutation of the 2^{2r+1} possible local neighborhoods can be achieved by composing reversible CA rules. For r = 1 (elementary CAs), G(1, {0, 1}) is a proper subgroup of S_8, and its structure is related to the 256 elementary CA rules. Conjecture: G(1, {0, 1}) has order 8! / 4 = 10080, consisting of the permutations that commute with the shift operator. Test: enumerate all 256 elementary CA rules, identify the reversible ones (Rule 15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240), compute the group generated by their local rules, and verify the structure. Impact: reversible CAs form a group whose structure determines the landscape of reversible computation.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a CA rule f of radius r as f: {0,1}^{2r+1} -> {0,1}. The Wolfram number of f is N = sum_{x=0}^{2^{2r+1}-1} f(x) * 2^x. A CA is reversible iff its global function F: {0,1}^Z -> {0,1}^Z is bijective. Hedlund's theorem: F is bijective iff the local rule is a permutation of neighborhoods that preserves the shift. For r=1: there are 2^8 = 256 rules. The reversible ones are: Rule 15, 51, 85, 170, 204, 240 (6 rules). Their local rules as permutations: Rule 170 = left shift (identity on neighborhoods), Rule 15 = NOT(left shift), Rule 51 = complement, Rule 85 = NOT(right shift), Rule 204 = identity (trivial), Rule 240 = right shift. These generate a subgroup of S_8. Conjecture: this subgroup is isomorphic to S_4 (the symmetry group of the square) acting on the 4 non-trivial neighborhoods. For r >= 2: G(r, {0,1}) is conjectured to be S_{2^{2r+1}}, meaning any permutation of neighborhoods is achievable by composing reversible CA rules. Test: compute the group generated by the reversible elementary CA rules using GAP or similar, verify the structure.
directions.title: Galois Theory of Cellular Automata: Which Rules Have Reversible Dynamics?
